papers.title_zh: 印度的家庭户主地位和儿童营养和免疫覆盖范围内的机会不平等
papers.source_body_en: This study explores the inequality of opportunity in nutrition and immunisation coverage among Indian children, with particular attention to household headship, using the most recent National Family Health Survey (NFHS)-5 (2019–2021) on children’s health indicators. Children’s health status was assessed through indicators such as stunting (height-for-age Z -score < −2), wasting (weight-for-height Z -score < −2), being underweight (weight-for-age Z -score < −2) and immunisation coverage (Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) vaccine, diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTaP) vaccine, polio vaccine and measles vaccine). Children aged 0–59 months were included for nutritional assessment, and those aged 12–23 months were considered for immunisation. The study constructs the Human Opportunity Index to measure the inequality of opportunity considering household headship and employs Shapley decomposition to analyse the contributing factors to such an inequality. The findings reveal that households headed by women are more vulnerable to stunting in children compared to those led by men. Furthermore, children from the higher-income groups were observed to have a much lower chance of experiencing stunting, wasting or being underweight. Wealth status is also positively and significantly associated with immunisation coverage. The study shows that household wealth significantly shapes children’s health opportunities, reducing malnutrition and enhancing immunisation outcomes. Sanitation contributes to disparities in nutritional outcomes, particularly among underweight (18.8%) and wasted (17%) children. Religious beliefs were found to influence wasting in children (16.9%) and immunisation choices of households (21.8%), while female-headed households show modest effects (4% on wasting, 1.3% on stunting).
papers.abstract_zh: 本研究利用关于儿童健康指标的最新国家家庭健康调查 (NFHS)-5(2019-2021),探讨了印度儿童在营养和免疫覆盖率方面的机会不平等,特别关注户主。通过发育迟缓(年龄别身高 Z 值 < -2)、消瘦(身高别体重 Z 值 < -2)、体重不足(年龄别体重 Z 值 < -2)和免疫覆盖率(卡介苗 (BCG) 疫苗、白喉、破伤风和百日咳 (DTaP))等指标评估儿童的健康状况疫苗、脊髓灰质炎 疫苗 和 麻疹 疫苗)。0-59 个月的儿童被纳入营养评估,12-23 个月的儿童被考虑进行免疫接种。该研究构建了人类机会指数来衡量考虑家庭户主地位的机会不平等,并采用沙普利分解来分析造成这种不平等的因素。调查结果显示,与男性为户主的家庭相比,女性户主的家庭更容易出现儿童发育迟缓的情况。此外,据观察,来自高收入群体的儿童发育迟缓、消瘦或体重不足的可能性要低得多。财富状况也与免疫覆盖率呈显着正相关。研究表明,家庭财富可以显着影响儿童的健康机会,减少营养不良并提高免疫效果。卫生条件造成营养结果的差异,尤其是体重不足(18.8%)和消瘦(17%)儿童。研究发现,宗教信仰会影响儿童消瘦(16.9%)和家庭的免疫选择(21.8%),而女户主家庭的影响不大(4%对消瘦,1.3%对发育迟缓)。

papers.title: Maternal Knowledge of Childhood Immunization and Its Association with Full Immunization Status Among Mothers of Children Aged 12–23 Months in a Riverine Community of Rivers State, Nigeria
papers.abstract: Maternal knowledge is a modifiable determinant of childhood vaccination, yet little is known about its level among mothers in the riverine communities of the Niger Delta. This study assessed the level of maternal knowledge about immunisation and its association with full immunisation status among children aged 12–23 months in Asari-Toru Local Government Area (ASALGA), Rivers State, Nigeria. A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 374 mothers or primary caregivers selected through multistage sampling. Knowledge was measured with a 13-item interviewer-administered scale (score 0–13) and categorised as good (9–13), fair (5–8) or poor (0–4). Associations with full immunisation were examined using chi-square tests and binary logistic regression. Only 25.7% of mothers had good knowledge, 48.7% had fair knowledge and 25.7% had poor knowledge. Although 93.0% had heard of childhood immunisation, only 49.2% knew the age for measles vaccination. Full immunisation coverage was 52.1%, 30.8% and 16.7% among children of mothers with good, fair and poor knowledge, respectively (p < 0.001). Good knowledge remained independently associated with full immunisation (AOR = 5.22; 95% CI: 2.46–11.08). Awareness of immunisation is high, but specific, actionable knowledge of the schedule is deficient and is associated with incomplete vaccination. Schedule-specific, culturally adapted health education delivered beyond clinic walls should be prioritised in riverine communities.
papers.journal: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MEDICAL EVALUATION AND PHYSICAL REPORT

A cross-sectional survey of 374 mothers revealed that only 25.7% had good knowledge, 48.7% had fair knowledge, and 25.7% had poor knowledge. Full immunisation coverage was significantly higher among children of mothers with good knowledge (52.1%) compared to those with fair (30.8%) or poor (16.7%) knowledge. These findings underscore the importance of targeted health education to improve vaccination rates in such communities. The study's cross-sectional design limits its ability to establish causality, and the evidence is considered moderate in strength due to the reliance on self-reported data.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 母亲知识是儿童 疫苗接种 的一个可改变的决定因素,但人们对尼日尔三角洲河流社区母亲的知识水平知之甚少。本研究旨在评估12-23月龄儿童的母亲免疫知识水平及其与充分免疫状态的关系。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 一项基于社区的横断面研究对 2023 年至 2024 年间在尼日利亚河流州 Asari-Toru 地方政府区 (ASALGA) 通过多阶段抽样选出的 374 名母亲或主要照顾者进行了研究。
elements_zh.methods: 知识采用包含 13 个项目的访谈员管理量表(分数 0-13)进行测量,并分为良好(9-13)、一般(5-8)或差(0-4)。使用卡方检验和二元逻辑回归检查与完全免疫的关联。
elements_zh.main_results: 只有25.7%的母亲知识良好,48.7%的母亲知识一般,25.7%的母亲知识较差。知识良好、一般和较差的母亲的孩子的完全免疫覆盖率分别为 52.1%、30.8% 和 16.7% (p < 0.001)。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 良好的知识仍然与完全免疫独立相关(AOR = 5.22;95% CI:2.46–11.08)。该研究强调需要进行有针对性的健康教育以提高 疫苗接种 率。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,提高母亲对特定 疫苗接种 时间表的了解可以提高河流社区的免疫覆盖率。这对旨在提高 疫苗接种 比率的公共卫生策略具有影响。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到横截面设计的限制,无法确定因果关系。由于依赖自我报告数据且缺乏纵向随访,证据强度中等。

papers.full_text: Abstract Skin diseases such as Monkeypox, Chickenpox, Measles, and other dermatological conditions pose significant challenges for accurate and timely diagnosis due to their visual similarity and variability in lesion presentation. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) systems leveraging AI have emerged as powerful tools to assist in the early and accurate detection of diseases like Monkeypox, enabling improved healthcare outcomes. This study introduces a novel approach for multi-class skin disease diagnosis. The methodology utilizes the Swin Transformer (ST) as a feature extractor, leveraging its ability to capture complex visual patterns in high-dimensional image data. Feature selection (FS) methods, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Mutual Information, Chi-square (\(\chi ^2\)), and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), are applied to identify the most relevant features, reducing noise and computational overhead. These optimized features are then classified using a range of machine learning classifiers, including Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Naive Bayes (NB). Among these, the combination of \(\chi ^2\) with RF and RFE with RF consistently achieves the highest diagnostic accuracy. The performance of this approach is rigorously evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation. The proposed method achieves 98.31% accuracy, 98.31% recall, 98.36% precision, and 98.33% F1-score using \(\chi ^2\) and RFE with Random Forest on original images. This represents a 4.44% improvement in accuracy compared to previous models. These results demonstrate that combining effective feature extraction and selection techniques with robust classifiers provides a highly accurate and efficient solution for automated skin disease diagnosis. analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the challenges of accurately diagnosing Monkeypox and other visually similar skin diseases, which have been a significant public health concern due to their clinical resemblance and variability in lesion presentation.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study employed a deep learning framework for automated skin disease diagnosis, focusing on Monkeypox using a dataset of skin images. The methodology involved feature extraction and selection techniques to enhance diagnostic accuracy.
analysis.methods: The study used the Swin Transformer for feature extraction and applied feature selection methods such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Mutual Information, Chi-square (\(\chi^2\)), and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) to identify relevant features. These optimized features were then classified using machine learning classifiers including Random Forest (RF), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Naive Bayes (NB).
analysis.main_results: The proposed method achieved 98.31% accuracy, 98.31% recall, 98.36% precision, and 98.33% F1-score using \(\chi^2\) and RFE with Random Forest on original images. This represents a 4.44% improvement in accuracy compared to previous models.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these results as demonstrating the effectiveness of combining feature extraction and selection techniques with robust classifiers for automated Monkeypox diagnosis. analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide a highly accurate and efficient solution for automated Monkeypox diagnosis, which can aid in early detection and improve healthcare outcomes, particularly in resource-limited settings where rapid and reliable diagnostic tools are essential.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's results are based on a dataset of skin images, and while the methodology is robust, the generalizability to real-world clinical settings may be limited. analysis.summary_en: This study introduces a novel deep learning framework for Monkeypox diagnosis using the Swin Transformer and feature selection techniques. The research addresses the challenges of accurately distinguishing Monkeypox from other skin diseases due to their visual similarity. The methodology combines feature extraction with various selection methods to enhance diagnostic accuracy. The results show a significant improvement in accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score compared to previous models. The authors interpret these findings as demonstrating the effectiveness of integrating advanced feature extraction with robust classifiers for automated diagnosis. The study's implications suggest that this approach can improve early detection and healthcare outcomes. However, the evidence is moderate due to the reliance on a single dataset and the lack of direct clinical validation, which may limit generalizability.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决准确诊断猴痘和其他视觉上相似的皮肤病的挑战,由于它们的临床相似性和病变表现的多样性,这些疾病一直是一个重大的公共卫生问题。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究采用了自动皮肤病 诊断 的深度学习框架,重点关注使用皮肤图像数据集的猴痘。该方法涉及特征提取和选择技术以提高诊断准确性。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究使用 Swin Transformer 进行特征提取,并应用主成分分析 (PCA)、互信息、卡方 (\(\chi^2\)) 和递归特征消除 (RFE) 等特征选择方法来识别相关特征。然后使用机器学习分类器对这些优化后的特征进行分类,包括随机森林 (RF)、支持 媒介 机器 (SVM)、极限梯度提升 (XGBoost) 和朴素贝叶斯 (NB)。
elements_zh.main_results: 该方法使用 \(\chi^2\) 和带有随机森林的 RFE 在原始图像上实现了 98.31% 的准确率、98.31% 的召回率、98.36% 的精度和 98.33% 的 F1 分数。与之前的模型相比,准确率提高了 4.44%。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些结果解释为证明了将特征提取和选择技术与稳健的分类器相结合以实现自动化 Monkeypox 诊断 的有效性。新颖之处在于 Swin Transformer 与特征选择方法的集成,以提高诊断性能。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现为自动化猴痘 诊断 提供了高度准确和高效的解决方案,有助于早期检测并改善医疗保健结果,特别是在资源有限的环境中,快速可靠的诊断工具至关重要。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的结果基于皮肤图像数据集,虽然该方法很稳健,但对现实临床环境的普遍适用性可能有限。由于依赖单一数据集并且缺乏直接的临床验证,证据是中等的。

news.content_title: Wastewater surveillance expands to include multiple pathogens, including measles virus
news.content: Public Health Newswire from The Nation’s Health brings you the news you need now Public Health Newswire Wastewater surveillance expands to include multiple pathogens, including measles virus November 4, 2026 Mark Barna Wastewater monitoring to jump-start prevention of infectious outbreaks has expanded in the U.S. in recent years. At a Tuesday session, “ Wastewater-based Epidemiology: Advances and Future Direction in Wastewater Surveillance ,” experts discussed how the practice has grown into a surveillance juggernaut, in which scientists test for multiple pathogens, including the measles virus, to prompt timely public health action. U.S. surveillance increased during the COVID-19 pandemic as wastewater testing ramped up for SARS-CoV-2. These days, public health officials are testing locally for a long list of viruses to prevent or mitigate outbreaks. Among them are RSV, influenza, norovirus, mpox, foodborne illnesses and even antimicrobial resistance pathogens. As of Nov. 1, over 4,800 cases of measles have been reported in the U.S. this year, and more states are monitoring wastewater for the measles virus. California, which this year has had 59 measles cases, tests wastewater for the pathogen at 89 sites in 39 counties. Officials have found a correlation between positive tests and measles cases. “Wastewater surveillance may be effective in identifying presence of measles, complementing case surveillance and guiding public health response,” said Mariah Otstot of the California Department of Public Health. North Carolina monitors wastewater for five pathogens at 36 sites in 29 counties. The state added measles testing in June 2025. It has had four wastewater measles detections, along with 24 documented measles cases in 10 counties, according to data at the North Carolina Department of Health . A correlation in test sites and measles infections has been found. Department workers have created extensive communication messaging programs in infected areas. Three-quarters of wastewater detections occurred within four days of the symptom onset in communities. A detection without a reported case prompted the opening of a community vaccination clinic. Because North Carolina is mostly rural, only about half the population is on sewer systems. The rest use private septic tanks as their primary household wastewater treatment. That impedes pathogen detection in wastewater because there is no current way to monitor private septic tanks for pathogens, said Nicole Snyder, an epidemiologist at the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services. Snyder was not confident things would change in the conservative state. “Different people are more receptive or less receptive to” a government employee surveilling homeowner septic tanks, Snyder said. Antimicrobial resistance — when bacteria and viruses adapt effective shields against antibiotics and antivirals — is an urgent public health threat. Nearly 51,000 people die in the U.S. each year because of resistance, according ot the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. A chief culprit are resistant microbes in livestock finding their way into humans through the food supply. Colorado has begun a pilot program that monitors wastewater at nine sites for resistant pathogens. Beginning in 2025, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment tested about 2,000 wastewater samples, finding significant correlation between wastewater detections and prevalence of antimicrobial resistance in a region. A second correlation involved finding specific resistant pathogens in regions where the relevant livestock is raised. For example, OXA-48-like enzymes, which have been connected to antimicrobial resistance and found in hogs, were detected in regions where hog farming is common. “OXA-48-like had the greatest proportion of samples, increasing in eight regions,” said Eve Curran, a health professional at the department. The pilot program is planning to generate additional community monitoring and hospital wastewater sampling, Curran said. Photo by Onuma Inthapong, courtesy iStockphoto. analysis.brief_en: The American Public Health Association reports that wastewater surveillance for measles virus has expanded in the U.S., including testing in multiple states. This practice, which began during the COVID-19 pandemic, is now used to detect a range of pathogens, including measles, to guide public health responses. In North Carolina, testing for measles was added in June 2025, and four wastewater detections have been recorded alongside 24 documented cases in 10 counties. Officials have found a correlation between positive tests and measles cases, with three-quarters of detections occurring within four days of symptom onset. A detection without a reported case prompted the opening of a community vaccination clinic. However, the effectiveness of wastewater surveillance is limited in rural areas where many residents use private septic tanks, which cannot be monitored for pathogens. The practice is seen as a valuable tool to complement case surveillance and prevent outbreaks, with plans to expand monitoring in the future.

analysis.brief_en: The American Hospital Association reported on November 6, 2026, that Wisconsin has recorded its first measles-related death, while Pennsylvania has announced its sixth case of measles. This comes as measles cases are rising nationally. The report highlights the severity of the situation but does not provide specific details on the investigation, testing, or response measures taken. The evidence does not mention any explicit risk level or further actions being implemented. The information is based on official statements from the AHA, which serves as the source of the report.

analysis.time: ‘Quite unusual’: Adults make up two-thirds of measles cases in Pennsylvania, presenting unique challenges Meghan Holohan A large unvaccinated population plus waning herd immunity created the perfect conditions for the virus to infect adults.
analysis.location_and_population: Pennsylvania, United States; unvaccinated population.
analysis.event: Adults make up two-thirds of measles cases in Pennsylvania, highlighting unique challenges in managing the outbreak. The CDC has confirmed 4 measles-related deaths in the US this year, while at least 8 have been reported.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Pennsylvania reports 1,467 measles cases, with the outbreak being the epicenter of US measles activity. At least 8 people in the US have died from measles complications this year, though the CDC has confirmed only 4. The outbreak is attributed to a large unvaccinated population and waning herd immunity.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The outbreak is under investigation, with efforts to manage the spread through public health alerts and awareness campaigns. The CDC is monitoring the situation, and the US government is advised to improve vaccine acceptance and public health preparedness.

analysis.brief_en: A recent report highlights that adults account for two-thirds of measles cases in Pennsylvania, presenting unique challenges in outbreak management. The CDC has confirmed 4 measles-related deaths in the US this year, while at least 8 have been reported. Pennsylvania remains the epicenter of measles activity with 1,467 cases. The outbreak is attributed to a large unvaccinated population and waning herd immunity. Public health officials are investigating the spread and emphasizing the need for improved vaccine acceptance and preparedness. The situation underscores the importance of addressing vaccine hesitancy and strengthening community immunity to prevent further complications and deaths.

OffOn Stream on Wellness What parents need to know as measles outbreaks spread across the US New measles death in Wisconsin CDC ByYi-Jin Yu November 6, 2026, 5:24 PM More measles cases are being reported across the U.S., and eight people have died so far, including an infant in Wisconsin, the first measles-related death in the state since 1990, according to health officials. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there have been nearly 5,200 measles cases across 45 states and Washington, D.C., so far this year, as more have decided to opt out of vaccination. "I'm extremely concerned, and the reason for that is there's no indication that these outbreaks will be slowing down at this point," Dr. Andrew Handel, a pediatric infectious diseases physician at Stony Brook Children's Hospital in Stony Brook, New York, told ABC News. As the measles virus continues to spread, here's what parents should know about the disease. What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause acute respiratory illness, according to the CDC. It is more contagious that other respiratory viruses, such as the common cold, the flu or COVID. "It is the most contagious infection that we know of," Handel said. "The estimate is that for every person who has measles, they can infect up to 18 people who are unvaccinated with it." The measles virus in an image from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website. CDC Measles is spread through the air when someone infected with the virus exhales or coughs. People can also become infected after breathing in contaminated air or by touching an infected surface and then touching their eyes, noses or mouths, the CDC states. "For measles, it spreads through airborne means, which means that once [an infected person breathes] it out, it actually stays circulating in the air for up to two hours after they leave that room," Handel explained. "If someone goes to their doctor to be checked for measles, and they don't recognize that they have measles, and then they walk out of the room, someone who comes in an hour and a half later can become infected with measles." What are the symptoms of measles? The CDC notes that measles can initially look like other respiratory infections, with symptoms including a cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis (red, watery eyes), or a high fever, which can increase to more than 104 degrees Fahrenheit. The most recognizable symptom of measles is a rash that typically starts at the head and moves down the body. "People break out into the rash, which starts as red, dark circles that usually start right at the hairline and work their way down the body," Handel said. "As it works its way down, you see the red circles, the red dots further down. But the place where it started -- so, on the face -- the redness will start to come together, so it'll look like a sheet of redness, and it, again, starts from the head and works its way down, which is very particular." Related Measles cases surpass 5,000 in the US with infections confirmed in 45 states: CDC "We also see something called Koplik spots, which are usually whitish, bluish dots that can appear on the inside of the cheek," Handel added. "Those tend to come up a couple days before the rash, so it can help us to make the diagnosis a bit earlier." Popular Reads What to know about recounts in Mississippi with razor-thin margin in Senate race 2 days ago Kimmarie Johnson, 'Beverly Hills, 90210' actress, dies after heart emergency at 50 1 day ago Captain identified after deadly Florida Learjet crash Nov 3 Measles symptoms typically begin seven to 14 days after initial contact with the virus, according to the CDC. What are the complications of measles? A common misconception about measles, as the CDC notes, is that infection with the virus isn't severe. The CDC and Handel both stress that measles infections can give rise to serious complications, from short-term issues like diarrhea and ear infections, to serious to life-threatening long-term problems and death. "Many children, many people can go on and have complications ... that can include severe pneumonias, dehydration, and also acute brain infections, where suddenly, you can have seizures," Handel said. He continued, "You can have changes in behavior. You can develop meningitis where there's neck pain and headache because the measles infection [has] infiltrated into the spinal fluid. There are some children who, especially if they're infected before they turn 1 year old, in particular, can develop a neurologic progressive disease [called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE,] that ultimately results in death up to 10 years later. And so, there are some really scary outcomes from it." Related As measles continues to spread, health officials are seeing vaccine interest rise How can measles be prevented? According to the CDC, the best way to protect against measles is with the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine, or MMR, which can be administered to children starting at 12 months old. Children who receive a first dose of the MMR vaccine then need to get a second dose when they are between 4 and 6 years old. "The only way to prevent infections when there is an ongoing national outbreak at levels that we haven't seen in decades is to get the MMR vaccine," Handel said. "It is safe, it is effective, and it's the best thing we can do again to stop this outbreak and get the country back to the rates of measles infections that we'd previously seen." Not everyone may be able to get an MMR vaccine, such as children with cancer, those who are pregnant, and people who have compromised immune systems, so it is important to discuss your children's and family's eligibility and concerns with a medical provider. analysis.brief_en: A child in Wisconsin has died from measles, the first such death in the state since 1990, according to a report by STAT. The incident highlights concerns about declining vaccine coverage and the potential resurgence of the disease. The Wisconsin health department is investigating the case, but no specific containment measures or risk levels have been mentioned. This event underscores the importance of maintaining high vaccination rates to prevent outbreaks and protect vulnerable populations. The death serves as a reminder of the ongoing public health challenges related to measles, particularly in areas with lower immunization rates. The report emphasizes the need for continued vigilance and education to ensure community immunity.

analysis.brief_en: As of November 6, 2026, Pennsylvania is experiencing its largest measles outbreak in decades, with over 1,000 cases reported. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed this alarming trend, highlighting the severity of the situation. The outbreak has raised concerns about public health and vaccination rates, as measles is a highly contagious viral disease that can lead to serious complications. Authorities are working to contain the spread through monitoring and implementing preventive measures. The CDC's report underscores the need for increased vaccination efforts and public awareness to mitigate the impact of the outbreak. This event is part of a broader trend of measles resurgence in the United States, emphasizing the importance of maintaining high immunization coverage to prevent further spread.

Microscopy is courtesy of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control; layout, colorization and visual effects by National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. Reading Time: 3 minutes Wisconsin health officials reported the death of an infant related to the ongoing measles outbreak in southwestern Wisconsin. It’s the first measles-associated death in the state in more than 35 years, according to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. DHS reported that the coroner listed measles as the immediate cause of death. State officials said no further information about the death is being released to protect the privacy of the child and the family. DHS Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement that her “heart is broken for the family.” “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Johnson said in the statement. “Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.” Doctors recommend children get their first dose of the vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, between 12 and 15 months. But Dr. Ryan Westergaard, DHS chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases, announced Thursday on a call with reporters that the state is now recommending infants who are 6 months to 11 months old receive an early dose of the shot if they are at an increased risk of exposure due to the outbreak. “In an outbreak, when we know that an infant may be exposed to measles, there is a benefit to providing that protection earlier,” Westergaard said. “For families with babies younger than 6 months or others who cannot be vaccinated, the most important protection is making sure that the people around them are immune. That’s one of the reasons that maintaining high vaccination coverage is so important.” Kids younger than 5 years old are among those most at risk of serious complications from measles, along with people who are pregnant and those with weakened immune systems. The highly contagious virus can cause pneumonia and swelling of the brain. Westergaard said the red, bumpy rash associated with measles doesn’t usually occur until several days after someone becomes sick. He told reporters than an infection typically starts with fever, cough, runny nose, and red eyes, and he urged people to avoid contact with others as soon as these symptoms occur. “We need people to recognize measles infections when they do occur and do everything we can to avoid exposing others,” said Westergaard, adding that those with symptoms should contact their local health department or medical provider for further guidance. Related Stories Low vaccination rates drive southwest Wisconsin measles outbreak Measles is in Wisconsin. Are Milwaukee schools vulnerable? ‘I would never wish it on anyone:’ Measles resurgence spurs memories of past toll in Wisconsin Measles has made it to Wisconsin. Here’s what to know about the virus. There have been 431 measles cases across 13 Wisconsin counties as of Tuesday. It’s the highest number of cases in the state in more than 35 years, according to DHS. And it’s “almost certainly an underestimate” of infections, according to Westergaard. He told reporters that not everyone who becomes infected gets tested or comes to the attention of public health. Westergaard pointed out that widespread vaccination changed measles from a common childhood infection to a relatively rare disease until recent years. “That was an extraordinary public health achievement, but it wasn’t permanent and it wasn’t inevitable that we would have that success,” he said. “It depended on doing the hard work of maintaining high levels of immunity in our communities. The death we’re reporting today is a tragic reminder of what can happen when measles begins circulating again.” The vast majority of cases in Wisconsin this year have been linked to spread of the virus among residents of Grant, Iowa, Lafayette and Vernon counties. The remaining measles cases have been linked to people being infected with measles during travel out of state. So far, nine Wisconsinites have required hospitalization for severe symptoms from measles. Over 99% of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been four other measles-related deaths reported in the U.S. this year. The MMR vaccine is 97% effective at preventing measles when the person has completed the medically recommended two-dose course. State health officials are urging residents to check their and their families’ vaccination status through the state’s online registry or with their medical provider. DHS reported some progress on improving the state’s vaccination rates. Since Aug. 1, the state has delivered 2,000 doses of the MMR vaccine to local health departments in measles-affected communities. Across the state, over 42,000 doses of the vaccine have been administered since Aug. 1. This story was originally published by WPR. Microscopy is courtesy of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control; layout, colorization and visual effects by National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases. Reading Time: 3 minutes Wisconsin health officials reported the death of an infant related to the ongoing measles outbreak in southwestern Wisconsin. It’s the first measles-associated death in the state in more than 35 years, according to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services. DHS reported that the coroner listed measles as the immediate cause of death. State officials said no further information about the death is being released to protect the privacy of the child and the family. DHS Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement that her “heart is broken for the family.” “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Johnson said in the statement. “Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.” Doctors recommend children get their first dose of the vaccine for measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, between 12 and 15 months. But Dr. Ryan Westergaard, DHS chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases, announced Thursday on a call with reporters that the state is now recommending infants who are 6 months to 11 months old receive an early dose of the shot if they are at an increased risk of exposure due to the outbreak. “In an outbreak, when we know that an infant may be exposed to measles, there is a benefit to providing that protection earlier,” Westergaard said. “For families with babies younger than 6 months or others who cannot be vaccinated, the most important protection is making sure that the people around them are immune. That’s one of the reasons that maintaining high vaccination coverage is so important.” Kids younger than 5 years old are among those most at risk of serious complications from measles, along with people who are pregnant and those with weakened immune systems. The highly contagious virus can cause pneumonia and swelling of the brain. Westergaard said the red, bumpy rash associated with measles doesn’t usually occur until several days after someone becomes sick. He told reporters than an infection typically starts with fever, cough, runny nose, and red eyes, and he urged people to avoid contact with others as soon as these symptoms occur. “We need people to recognize measles infections when they do occur and do everything we can to avoid exposing others,” said Westergaard, adding that those with symptoms should contact their local health department or medical provider for further guidance. Related Stories Low vaccination rates drive southwest Wisconsin measles outbreak Measles is in Wisconsin. Are Milwaukee schools vulnerable? ‘I would never wish it on anyone:’ Measles resurgence spurs memories of past toll in Wisconsin Measles has made it to Wisconsin. Here’s what to know about the virus. There have been 431 measles cases across 13 Wisconsin counties as of Tuesday. It’s the highest number of cases in the state in more than 35 years, according to DHS. And it’s “almost certainly an underestimate” of infections, according to Westergaard. He told reporters that not everyone who becomes infected gets tested or comes to the attention of public health. Westergaard pointed out that widespread vaccination changed measles from a common childhood infection to a relatively rare disease until recent years. “That was an extraordinary public health achievement, but it wasn’t permanent and it wasn’t inevitable that we would have that success,” he said. “It depended on doing the hard work of maintaining high levels of immunity in our communities. The death we’re reporting today is a tragic reminder of what can happen when measles begins circulating again.” The vast majority of cases in Wisconsin this year have been linked to spread of the virus among residents of Grant, Iowa, Lafayette and Vernon counties. The remaining measles cases have been linked to people being infected with measles during travel out of state. So far, nine Wisconsinites have required hospitalization for severe symptoms from measles. Over 99% of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been four other measles-related deaths reported in the U.S. this year. The MMR vaccine is 97% effective at preventing measles when the person has completed the medically recommended two-dose course. State health officials are urging residents to check their and their families’ vaccination status through the state’s online registry or with their medical provider. DHS reported some progress on improving the state’s vaccination rates. Since Aug. 1, the state has delivered 2,000 doses of the MMR vaccine to local health departments in measles-affected communities. Across the state, over 42,000 doses of the vaccine have been administered since Aug. 1. This story was originally published by WPR. news.content_title: Canada’s Measles Outbreak Concentrated Among Undervaccinated
news.content: Your Clinical Hub News & Perspective Tools & Reference CME/CE More EN RegisterLog In Ask AI Search AI Mode Medscape News Canada Canada’s Measles Outbreak Concentrated Among Undervaccinated Marilynn Larkin November 06, 2026 2 Add to Email Alerts The outbreak that contributed to Canada’s loss of its measles elimination status was concentrated in undervaccinated communities, highlighting the risk for measles resurgence even in countries that previously controlled the disease, researchers warn. The outbreak started in October 2024 and was officially declared over on October 19. But Canada’s measles elimination status, which was first achieved in 1998, can be regained only after the current strain is stopped for at least 12 consecutive months. Meanwhile, Canada has learned “several important public health lessons” from the study, Sarah Wilson, MD, deputy chief of medical and systems support at Public Health Ontario in Toronto, told Medscape News Canada. The analysis of measles cases reported to Ontario’s public health surveillance system during the outbreak found that high vaccination coverage provides important population-level protection, she said. “Despite the size of the outbreak, spread into the broader population was limited, demonstrating the protection associated with high vaccine acceptance.” Sarah Wilson, MD Nevertheless, “persistent immunity gaps can allow measles to spread rapidly,” said Wilson. “In Ontario, about 90% of outbreak cases occurred in historically undervaccinated communities, and 89% were among people who were unvaccinated. This [finding] reinforces the importance of identifying and closing immunity gaps before an imported case can lead to sustained transmission.” Overall, she said, the outbreak “highlighted the importance of sustained, culturally appropriate engagement and adapting the response to the needs of affected communities, including trusted communications, lower-barrier testing, and flexible vaccination approaches such as community-based clinics and home visits.” SUGGESTED FOR YOU The study was published online on October 28 in The BMJ. Public Health Achievements Fragile Researchers gathered demographic characteristics, vaccination status, hospital admissions, complications, pregnancy-associated outcomes, mortality, and evidence of international spread for the cohort of measles cases reported to Ontario’s public health surveillance system during the outbreak. Cases were identified using an outbreak-specific definition incorporating epidemiologic, clinical, laboratory, and viral sequencing criteria. Phylogenetic analysis of measles virus sequences was used to assess evidence of spread to other countries. The outbreak included 2377 cases (2064 confirmed and 313 probable) over 49 weeks. Most cases (90.3%) occurred among members of established undervaccinated communities, with limited spillover into the broader population. “The finding that stood out to us was just how concentrated the outbreak remained within communities with longstanding low immunization coverage, despite the very large number of cases and the extraordinary infectiousness of measles,” Wilson said. “In some ways, that is reassuring because it demonstrates the population-level protection provided by high vaccine coverage. At the same time, it shows how substantial immunity gaps within particular communities can allow measles to spread for a prolonged period, even in a country where overall vaccine acceptance remains relatively high.” Approximately 73% of cases occurred in individuals aged 19 years or younger; 89.2% of infected patients were unvaccinated, and 4.1% had unknown vaccination status. The outbreak was associated with 166 (7%) hospital admissions, 13 (< 1%) admissions to an ICU, 51 (2.1%) infections during pregnancy, 10 (< 1%) congenital measles infections, one (< 1%) case of encephalitis, and one (< 1%) infant death. The researchers were struck by the impact on pregnant individuals and young infants, Wilson said. “The outbreak highlighted that longstanding immunity gaps can persist into adulthood and have consequences beyond childhood disease.” In addition, the sequencing analysis identified a novel N450 distinct sequence identifier that was subsequently detected in other countries, including the US, Mexico, and Netherlands. In a related editorial, Jennifer B. Nuzzo, DrPH, director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, Rhode Island, warned, “Canada’s experience underscores the fragility of hard-won public health achievements and the need for countries to recommit to elimination, not only to prevent needless illness and death but also to strengthen defenses against risk of infectious diseases more broadly.” Measles Not Consigned to the Past Regarding strategies to reverse low vaccine uptake and sustain culturally appropriate engagement, Wilson said, “There isn’t a single strategy that will work for every community. The reasons for longstanding low vaccine uptake are complex and can include structural barriers to accessing care, historical experiences with health systems, and community-specific perspectives on vaccination.” “What is important is sustained engagement rather than engagement that begins and ends when there is an outbreak,” she explained. “That means working with trusted community members and local healthcare providers to understand the specific barriers and concerns within a community, making vaccination convenient and accessible, and providing information in ways that are culturally and linguistically appropriate.” Clinicians can help by using routine healthcare encounters “as opportunities to review immunization status, identify people who may have missed doses, answer questions without judgment, and offer vaccination where appropriate,” she said. “Immunity gaps are not always immediately obvious. Someone may have missed vaccination many years ago and remain susceptible into adulthood. Clinicians can help close those gaps before someone is exposed to measles, rather than waiting until an outbreak occurs.” The practical message is simple, she said. “Don’t assume measles is a disease of the past. Maintaining high vaccine coverage, identifying people who remain susceptible, and considering measles when the clinical and epidemiologic picture fits remain important even in countries that have previously achieved elimination.” Brian Ward, MD Brian Ward, MD, professor of medicine at McGill University and senior scientist at the Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal, commented on the study for Medscape News Canada. “As long as large pockets of under- and unimmunized people exist and people continue to move around the world in airplanes, outbreaks like this will continue to occur,” he said. “Measles is one of the most transmissible human viruses (much more transmissible than influenza, for example), so even transient exposures can contribute to rapidly expanding chains of transmission in susceptible populations.” While Ward agreed that culturally appropriate engagement is needed, “This is far easier said than done,” he noted. “Trust takes time and effort to build in some communities. Identifying community ‘champions’ who can communicate in culturally sensitive ways and who are a priori trusted can be an effective approach.” Yet, he added, “These kinds of links with some communities can be difficult, if not impossible, to establish in the setting of an ongoing outbreak.” Clinicians can help by staying up to date on vaccine-preventable infections, taking every opportunity to review the vaccination status of individuals and promote vaccines, and “maintaining a high degree of suspicion for measles cases in susceptible populations so that appropriate resources can be mobilized as early as possible to keep the inevitable next outbreak as small as possible,” he said. “Given the level of misinformation about vaccines in general and about measles vaccination in particular, we have to be ready to take the time to offer a true narrative to hesitant parents,” he added. “Many antivaccine voices compare the dangers of vaccination to no illness, which has never been a fair comparison. Measles Can Cause Fatal Brain Disease Years After Recovery: Study Written By : Medha Baranwal ,Medically Reviewed By : Dr. Kamal Kant Kohli Published On 2026-11-05T20:00:41+05:30 | Updated On 6 Nov 2026 12:23 PM IST Philippines: Measles is not merely a rash-producing illness; it can cause serious complications even years after apparent recovery. A rare but almost invariably fatal neurological condition, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), can develop years after measles infection. A new report published in Emerging Infectious Diseases highlights this delayed complication, highlighting the importance of measles prevention through vaccination. The study, led by Maela P. Palisoc of the National Children’s Hospital, Quezon City, and the College of Medicine, San Beda University, Manila, Philippines, and colleagues, reviewed children diagnosed with SSPE over 16 years. The researchers warned that additional cases linked to the country's 2018–2019 measles outbreak could emerge in the coming years because of the long interval between infection and neurological symptoms. SSPE is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent infection of the central nervous system with a defective measles virus. It typically develops several years after measles infection, particularly when infection occurs during early childhood, and is almost always fatal. For the study, researchers retrospectively examined medical records of 20 children admitted with SSPE to the National Children’s Hospital between January 2007 and December 2022. They assessed clinical characteristics, vaccination history, reported measles infection, and the estimated timing of infection in relation to national measles outbreaks. The study findings revealed the following: Recent increase in admissions: Eight of the 20 children (40%) were admitted during 2020–2022, while five (25%) were admitted in 2022 alone. Cases linked to the latest outbreak: Four children had estimated measles infection dates corresponding to the 2018–2019 outbreak. All were admitted between 2020 and 2022, approximately 2.1–3.5 years after infection. Early childhood infection: The median age at reported measles illness was 0.7 years, while the median age at hospital admission was 6.2 years. Ten of the 19 children with an estimable age at infection had contracted measles before nine months of age. Incomplete measles history: A history of measles was reported in 15 children (75%), was unknown in four (20%), and was absent in one (5%). Vaccination history: Seventeen children (85%) had reportedly received at least one measles-containing vaccine, although 11 (55%) had received only one dose. Vaccination histories were based on parental or guardian recall and were not consistently verified against records. Declining measles vaccine coverage in the Philippines may have increased susceptibility to infection, with first-dose coverage falling to 64% in 2021 amid repeated outbreaks. The researchers recommended cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody testing in children with progressive neurological deterioration and myoclonus, even without a reported history of measles, to avoid missing SSPE diagnoses. The study was limited by its small, single-center sample, lack of population-level data, and reliance on recalled histories. The researchers emphasized strengthening SSPE surveillance and sustaining two-dose measles vaccination coverage to prevent future cases. Reference: Palisoc MP, Ramones MS, Jamora RDG. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis after measles outbreaks, the Philippines, 2007–2022. analysis.brief_en: A study published in Emerging Infectious Diseases reveals that measles can lead to a rare but almost always fatal neurological condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) years after recovery. Conducted in the Philippines, the research analyzed 20 children admitted to the National Children’s Hospital between 2007 and 2022, with 8 admitted during 2020–2022 and 5 in 2022 alone. Four of these cases were linked to the 2018–2019 measles outbreak, with infections estimated to have occurred 2.1–3.5 years prior. SSPE typically develops several years after measles infection, especially in early childhood, and is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. The study underscores the importance of measles prevention through vaccination and recommends cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody testing for children with neurological deterioration. It also highlights the need for improved SSPE surveillance and maintaining two-dose vaccination coverage. The research was limited by its small sample size, single-center focus, and reliance on parental recall for vaccination histories. The findings emphasize the long-term risks of measles infection and the critical role of vaccination in preventing such complications.

news.title_zh: 研究:麻疹 可能在康复数年后导致致命性脑部疾病
news.source_body_en: A study published in Emerging Infectious Diseases reveals that measles can lead to a rare but almost always fatal neurological condition called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) years after recovery. Conducted in the Philippines, the research analyzed 20 children admitted to the National Children’s Hospital between 2007 and 2022, with 8 admitted during 2020–2022 and 5 in 2022 alone. Four of these cases were linked to the 2018–2019 measles outbreak, with infections estimated to have occurred 2.1–3.5 years prior. SSPE typically develops several years after measles infection, especially in early childhood, and is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. The study underscores the importance of measles prevention through vaccination and recommends cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody testing for children with neurological deterioration. It also highlights the need for improved SSPE surveillance and maintaining two-dose vaccination coverage. The research was limited by its small sample size, single-center focus, and reliance on parental recall for vaccination histories. The findings emphasize the long-term risks of measles infection and the critical role of vaccination in preventing such complications.

news.content: An electron microscope image of a measles virus particle. (Cynthia S. Goldsmith; William Bellini, Ph.D./Centers for Disease Control and Prevention/TNS/TNS) By David Mowery | dmowery@readingeagle.com | Reading Eagle PUBLISHED: November 3, 2026 at 8:15 AM EST The statewide total of confirmed measles cases has reached 1,433 across 44 counties. Berks County continues to hold at seven cases in the update issued Monday by the sate Department of Health. The state is reporting five measles-associated deaths. The department’s update noted the following: • New positive cases since Oct. 30: 7 • Total counties: 44 • Total cumulative cases: 1,433 • Total hospitalizations: 269 • Total confirmed measles-associated deaths: 5 • Measles cases among vaccinated individuals: 4 (less than 1% of cases) According to the department’s dashboard at pa.gov/measles , Lancaster County remains at the top in cases with 496. Cases in the region: Chester County, 93; Lebanon County, 22; Schuylkill County, 7; Montgomery County, 3; and Lehigh County, 2. State health center staff have administered more than 6,800 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations at 238 pop-up vaccination clinics in affected communities since the outbreak began in late April, officials said. Overall, the department has given more than 10,600 MMR vaccine doses this year. Officials said healthcare providers continue to see an increase in residents interested in the MMR vaccinations. Providers typically administer about 25,000 doses of the vaccine a month. They said more than 56,000 doses were given in September and that more than 53,000 MMR vaccines were given in October. Because measles continues to spread, the department said it recommends an additional early zero dose for infants between the ages of 6 and 11 months who live in or travel to counties flagged on the measles dashboard for sustained community transmission. They said the early dose does not replace the two routine doses. Children 12 months and older who have not received any dose should get one now and a second dose at least 28 days later. Those who have two documented doses of MMR do not need another, the department said. Adults who have only one dose or cannot find their vaccination records should talk with a healthcare provider or pharmacist about getting vaccinated. Measles is spread when someone who is infected breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours after the infected person leaves the area, the department said. Symptoms begin with fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes (conjunctivitis), followed by a rash that starts on the head and spreads downward. Without proper protection or supportive care, measles can be deadly, officials said. Symptoms can start seven to 21 days after exposure. If you believe you were exposed to measles and are experiencing symptoms, you are advised to contact your healthcare provider or call the health department’s hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258). The state health department has administered over 6,800 measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccinations since the outbreak began in late April, with more than 10,600 doses given this year. Five measles-associated deaths have been recorded, and 269 hospitalizations have occurred. Measles spreads through respiratory droplets and remains infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to two hours. The department recommends an additional early zero dose for infants between 6 and 11 months in high-risk areas, though this does not replace the two routine doses. Adults with only one dose or no records should consult healthcare providers for vaccination. The outbreak continues to spread, prompting ongoing public health responses.

news.content: New York’s first measles death in 30 years is an omen of worse to come A child died after contracting the disease amid the largest national measles outbreak in more than three decades By Mary Randolph edited by Claire Cameron Join Our Community of Science Lovers! A child in upstate New York died on Monday after contracting measles . This marks the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, as the outbreak continues to spread across the country. In a statement, New York governor Kathy Hochul said she was “heartbroken” and that the death reflected a crisis of government and public health. Hochul declared measles a statewide disaster last month. With fewer immune protections, children are especially at risk for measles and its more dangerous effects. And as the outbreak surges, doctors are becoming increasingly concerned about congenital measles. If a pregnant woman has measles, there’s a 25 to 30 percent chance her child will also acquire measles, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. Congenital measles is not tracked by the Center for Disease Control and Prevention—the condition had become exceedingly rare, but rising rates are raising fears about its potential effects once more. If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today. As of October 29, the CDC had confirmed 4,852 measles cases across the U.S. so far this year. New York State has had a total of 178 confirmed cases, mainly concentrated in the central part of the state. According to officials, the recent death in New York occurred in Lewis County, which is northeast of Syracuse and has seen 16 cases in 2026. It is representative of a worsening national picture. The U.S. is currently in the thick of the worst measles outbreak since 1991. Case numbers this year have already doubled those of 2025 —previously the worst year for the disease since 1991. (The U.S. was declared measles-free in 2000.) Technically, the country still holds its measles-free status , a title that is marked by 12 months without continuous local transmission, although experts expect that may change soon. Officials are set to meet in the next few weeks to determine whether that status—hailed for years as a symbol of excellence in public health—should be revised or eliminated. As of October 30, the CDC has reported three deaths from measles nationally—although some states have reported deaths that have been disputed by the CDC—and an 11 percent hospitalization rate. In its milder forms, the disease can cause an itchy rash and fever, but it can also cause pneumonia and severe brain inflammation, which, without treatment, can prove fatal or disabling. The measles virus is the most contagious virus known—but it is not impossible to contain. Vaccines, particularly the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combined shot, had helped measles fade because of herd immunity. But dwindling vaccination rates are helping the disease break through, with dire consequences. The MMR jab offers 97 percent protection for life after two doses given in childhood and was the major factor in eradicating measles in the U.S. But with higher levels of vaccine skepticism among the public and the upper echelons of the Trump administration, fewer children are receiving the vaccine: in the past 10 years, MMR vaccination rates among kindergarteners have fallen from 94 percent to 92.4 percent. (A 95 percent vaccination rate is the critical number to ensure community or herd immunity.) Of the cases reported by the CDC this year, 96 percent were among people who were unvaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. It’s unclear whether the child that died on Monday was vaccinated. Editor’s Note (11/3/26): This is a breaking news story and may be updated. news.title_zh: 纽约30年来首例麻疹死亡预示着更糟糕的事情即将来临
news.source_body_en: A child in upstate New York died from measles on Monday, October 26, 2026, marking the first measles death in the state in 30 years. This incident is part of the largest measles outbreak in the U.S. since the 1990s, with the CDC reporting 4,852 confirmed cases as of October 29, 2026. New York State has seen 178 cases, mainly in its central region, and the death highlights the growing risk of measles due to declining vaccination rates. The child’s vaccination status remains unclear, and the outbreak has raised concerns about congenital measles, which can affect unborn children if a pregnant woman contracts the virus. Governor Kathy Hochul declared measles a statewide disaster and is preparing to meet with officials to assess the national measles-free status, which is currently under review. The outbreak has doubled case numbers from 2025, the worst year for measles since 1991, and experts warn of potential long-term health impacts. The CDC has reported three deaths nationally, with some states disputing these figures, and the situation remains under investigation.

(November 2, 2026) – Based on information currently available, the New York State Department of Health and Lewis County Public Health issued the following joint statement on the first known measles-associated death in New York State in more than 30 years: “We are deeply saddened by the death of a child in Lewis County associated with the ongoing measles outbreak. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the child’s family and loved ones and ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time. “Measles is a highly contagious disease that can cause serious complications and death. Vaccination is the best protection against measles. “The Department has offered resources to Lewis County to assist with community outreach and support local vaccination efforts – both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak. “We urge New Yorkers to ensure they are up to date on measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations and speak to their healthcare provider about immunizations.” Measles Prevention and Vaccine Information The news comes four weeks after Governor Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in response to the measles outbreak across areas of New York and neighboring states, expanding the pool of eligible individuals who can administer measles vaccines and providing swift access to additional resources if needed. The Department is working with county health departments and local partners to provide the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to any unvaccinated individuals who request it and to closely monitor and investigate all reported cases. Monitoring and investigation activities, such as contact tracing, are ways public health officials work to keep affected communities safe from the spread of infectious diseases. Anyone who is contacted during these activities is encouraged to be responsive so that important information can be shared to prevent more infections. As of October 24, there have been 178 total cases this year: 170 in New York State outside of the city, and eight in New York City. Apply in Person or email Shorts1280@yahoo.com All New Yorkers are urged to protect themselves by making sure they are up to date on their measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines and be aware of health advisories if traveling with unvaccinated individuals, especially young children. The latest guidance issued during this outbreak recommends that infants 6 months and older receive an early dose of the MMR vaccine for protection before travel or if they are otherwise at risk of being exposed, such as residence in a community with measles transmission. Measles is a highly contagious, serious respiratory disease that causes rash and fever. In some cases, measles can reduce the immune system’s ability to fight other infections like pneumonia. This disease is caused by a virus that is spread by coughing or sneezing into the air. Individuals can catch the disease by breathing in the virus or, less commonly, by touching a contaminated surface, then touching the eyes, nose, or mouth. Serious complications of measles include hospitalization, pneumonia, miscarriage, preterm birth, brain swelling, immune amnesia and death. Long-term serious complications can also include subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, a type of brain inflammation resulting from an earlier measles infection that can lead to permanent brain damage years after the initial infection. The best protection against measles is the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Those traveling domestically or internationally should plan to be fully vaccinated against measles at least two weeks before departure. One dose provides 93 percent protection while two doses provide 97 percent protection. Babies as young as 6 months should get one dose of the MMR vaccine if they are traveling abroad or to an area where measles is prevalent or if they reside in a community with measles transmission. These babies should then continue to get their next two MMR vaccines on schedule for a total of three vaccines. Anyone who is not protected can get measles if exposed and can easily spread it to others when they return home. The Department has released a health advisory for healthcare providers on clinical guidance for measles. A person with measles can pass it to others as soon as four days before a rash appears and as late as four days after the rash appears. The incubation period for measles is up to 21 days. People who are exposed to measles and not immune should quarantine for 21 days after exposure, and those who test positive should isolate until four days after the rash appears. Symptoms of measles can include the following: Seven to 14 days, and up to 21 days after a measles infection High fever Cough Runny nose Red, watery eyes A rash can occur 3-5 days after symptoms become apparent: The rash usually begins as flat red spots that appear on the face at the hairline and spread downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs and feet. Small, raised bumps may also appear on top of the flat red spots. The spots may become joined together as they spread from the head to the rest of the body. When the rash appears, a person’s fever may spike to more than 104° Fahrenheit. How Individuals Can Protect Themselves Individuals should check their vaccination status. Anyone who is unsure of their vaccination status should contact a healthcare provider or local health department. Know the symptoms. Measles often begins with fever, cough, runny nose, and red, watery eyes. A rash typically appears several days later, starting on the face and spreading across the body. Those who are sick should call ahead before visiting a clinic, urgent care, or emergency department so infection-control steps can be taken. Immunization Guidance The MMR vaccine is highly effective and the best protection against measles. Most people born before 1957 are considered immune because they were likely exposed to the virus. Those who received the vaccine between 1963 and 1967 may have received a vaccine that wasn’t as effective and should talk to their health care provider about getting revaccinated. Find the Department’s travel advisory urging New Yorkers to ensure they are fully vaccinated against measles before international travel or travel to an area in the U.S. experiencing an outbreak. Healthcare providers should report suspected measles cases to their local health department. Visit the Department’s dedicated measles website for information about measles, current case numbers, immunization data and information for providers. More information about the measles vaccine can be found here. Beth Mole – Nov 6, 2026 5:06 PM | 46 Boxes and vials of the Measles, Mumps, Rubella Virus Vaccine at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. Credit: Getty | Jan Sonnenmair Boxes and vials of the Measles, Mumps, Rubella Virus Vaccine at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. Credit: Getty | Jan Sonnenmair Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the first measles death in the state since 1990, officials reported Thursday. The death comes amid an outbreak in the Badger State that has stricken over 430 people across 13 counties this year. “Any death of a child is a tragedy, and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Wisconsin Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. “Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.” The baby’s death is the third measles fatality nationally just this week, following the death of a New York child reported on Monday and another death in Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday. The Pennsylvania death was of an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County; the state health department did not provide additional details, such as the age of the person. The state’s explosive, ongoing measles outbreak has led to 1,467 cases so far this year. In all, there have been nine reported measles deaths this year in the US, eight of which have been confirmed by state officials. The deaths include the baby’s death in Wisconsin, the child’s death in New York, and seven deaths (six confirmed) in Pennsylvania, including two babies, a healthy teen, and several adults with underlying health conditions. National context As of November 5, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 5,182 measles cases in the US this year across 47 states and jurisdictions. The CDC is reporting four measles deaths, though it’s unclear which of the reported deaths the CDC has counted. Ars Video What Happens to the Developers When AI Can Code? | Ars Frontiers The national case and death tallies are the highest recorded since 1991, though the reported cases likely represent a significant undercount of actual cases. As Wisconsin health officials noted in the announcement of the baby’s death, “Not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested, which means cases may go unreported.” This is particularly true given that large outbreaks, including the one ongoing in Pennsylvania, have struck in tight-knit religious communities that are less likely to seek conventional medical care. In 2000, the US declared measles eliminated after a year without continuous domestic transmission, thanks to high vaccination rates. The declaration was a public health triumph over the virus, which is among the most contagious on Earth. Prior to vaccination, measles sickened 3 to 4 million people per year, sending nearly 50,000 to the hospital, causing 1,000 cases of brain swelling, and killing 400 to 500 people. Amid slipping vaccination rates nationwide and the spread of anti-vaccine misinformation and rhetoric, the virus has come roaring back, and the country’s elimination status is likely to be stripped. Next week (November 10 to 13), a committee of infectious disease experts assembled by the Pan American Health Organization—a regional office for the World Health Organization—will review data from 2025 and early 2026 to assess if measles has reestablished in the US. Politicized public health Under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., much about the vaccine-preventable outbreaks has become political and contentious, including the definition and confirmation of measles-associated deaths. Amid the first deaths reported in Pennsylvania, Kennedy falsely suggested state officials “fabricated” the deaths and reportedly ordered the CDC to delete them from its national data. The CDC then changed the way it counts measles deaths, abandoning a long-standing practice of reporting state-confirmed deaths. Now, the CDC relies on federal death records, which take much longer to process and are not intended to provide real-time data during active outbreaks. The seventh, unconfirmed Pennsylvania death was reportedly of a 39-year-old woman in Franklin County; it was announced on October 12 by the county’s Coroner’s office. At the time, the coroner explicitly said the death met the state’s definition of a measles-associated death. Under the state’s criteria, a death is considered measles-associated if the person dies within 30 days of testing positive and shows clinical signs of infection, with no other significant cause for the death, such as a car crash. Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner listed the death as “a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles” and reported that the woman had recently been diagnosed with and treated for measles. In an email exchange with Ars Technica on Thursday, the state health department said it “has not found any Franklin County cases” that meet the state’s criteria but that “the investigation has not yet been closed.” The Franklin County coroner did not respond to a request for comment on the discrepancy. The Philadelphia Inquirer has taken legal action to obtain more information about the woman’s death, including her name, which was withheld by the coroner and sealed by a county judge. This post was updated to correct the name of the Franklin County Coroner. Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. Beth has a Ph.D. in microbiology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and attended the Science Communication program at the University of California, Santa Cruz. Beth Mole – Nov 6, 2026 5:06 PM | 46 Boxes and vials of the Measles, Mumps, Rubella Virus Vaccine at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. Credit: Getty | Jan Sonnenmair Boxes and vials of the Measles, Mumps, Rubella Virus Vaccine at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. Credit: Getty | Jan Sonnenmair Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only Learn more Minimize to nav An infant in Wisconsin has died of measles, the first measles death in the state since 1990, officials reported Thursday. The death comes amid an outbreak in the Badger State that has stricken over 430 people across 13 counties this year. “Any death of a child is a tragedy, and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease,” Wisconsin Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. “Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.” The baby’s death is the third measles fatality nationally just this week, following the death of a New York child reported on Monday and another death in Pennsylvania reported on Wednesday. The Pennsylvania death was of an unvaccinated person in Jefferson County; the state health department did not provide additional details, such as the age of the person. The state’s explosive, ongoing measles outbreak has led to 1,467 cases so far this year. In all, there have been nine reported measles deaths this year in the US, eight of which have been confirmed by state officials. The deaths include the baby’s death in Wisconsin, the child’s death in New York, and seven deaths (six confirmed) in Pennsylvania, including two babies, a healthy teen, and several adults with underlying health conditions. National context As of November 5, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is reporting 5,182 measles cases in the US this year across 47 states and jurisdictions. The CDC is reporting four measles deaths, though it’s unclear which of the reported deaths the CDC has counted. Ars Video What Happens to the Developers When AI Can Code? | Ars Frontiers The national case and death tallies are the highest recorded since 1991, though the reported cases likely represent a significant undercount of actual cases. As Wisconsin health officials noted in the announcement of the baby’s death, “Not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested, which means cases may go unreported.” This is particularly true given that large outbreaks, including the one ongoing in Pennsylvania, have struck in tight-knit religious communities that are less likely to seek conventional medical care. In 2000, the US declared measles eliminated after a year without continuous domestic transmission, thanks to high vaccination rates. The declaration was a public health triumph over the virus, which is among the most contagious on Earth. Prior to vaccination, measles sickened 3 to 4 million people per year, sending nearly 50,000 to the hospital, causing 1,000 cases of brain swelling, and killing 400 to 500 people. Amid slipping vaccination rates nationwide and the spread of anti-vaccine misinformation and rhetoric, the virus has come roaring back, and the country’s elimination status is likely to be stripped. Next week (November 10 to 13), a committee of infectious disease experts assembled by the Pan American Health Organization—a regional office for the World Health Organization—will review data from 2025 and early 2026 to assess if measles has reestablished in the US. Politicized public health Under anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., much about the vaccine-preventable outbreaks has become political and contentious, including the definition and confirmation of measles-associated deaths. Amid the first deaths reported in Pennsylvania, Kennedy falsely suggested state officials “fabricated” the deaths and reportedly ordered the CDC to delete them from its national data. The CDC then changed the way it counts measles deaths, abandoning a long-standing practice of reporting state-confirmed deaths. Now, the CDC relies on federal death records, which take much longer to process and are not intended to provide real-time data during active outbreaks. The seventh, unconfirmed Pennsylvania death was reportedly of a 39-year-old woman in Franklin County; it was announced on October 12 by the county’s Coroner’s office. At the time, the coroner explicitly said the death met the state’s definition of a measles-associated death. Under the state’s criteria, a death is considered measles-associated if the person dies within 30 days of testing positive and shows clinical signs of infection, with no other significant cause for the death, such as a car crash. Franklin County Coroner Jordan Conner listed the death as “a probable acute cardiac event due to possible complications of the measles” and reported that the woman had recently been diagnosed with and treated for measles. In an email exchange with Ars Technica on Thursday, the state health department said it “has not found any Franklin County cases” that meet the state’s criteria but that “the investigation has not yet been closed.” The Franklin County coroner did not respond to a request for comment on the discrepancy. The Philadelphia Inquirer has taken legal action to obtain more information about the woman’s death, including her name, which was withheld by the coroner and sealed by a county judge. This post was updated to correct the name of the Franklin County Coroner. Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth Mole Senior Health Reporter Beth is Ars Technica’s Senior Health Reporter. news.source_body_en: Wisconsin officials reported the death of a baby from measles, marking the first such death in the state since 1990. The baby's death is the third measles fatality nationally this week, following similar cases in New York and Pennsylvania. The CDC is tracking 5,182 measles cases in the US this year, the highest since 1991, though underreporting is likely due to limited medical care access in affected communities. The US declared measles eliminated in 2000, but recent outbreaks indicate a potential resurgence. Officials emphasize the importance of vaccination to prevent such preventable tragedies.
news.content_zh: 威斯康星州官员报告了一名婴儿死于 麻疹 的事件,这是该州自 1990 年以来首次发生此类死亡事件。该事件是威斯康星州正在进行的 麻疹 暴发 事件的一部分,该事件已影响到 13 个县的 430 多人。继纽约和宾夕法尼亚州发生类似案件后,这名婴儿的死亡是本周全国第三起 麻疹 死亡事件。CDC 今年追踪了美国 5,182 例 麻疹 病例,这是自 1991 年以来的最高水平,但漏报可能是由于受影响社区的医疗保健机会有限。美国于 2000 年宣布 麻疹 被淘汰,但最​​近的 麻疹 表明有可能卷土重来。官员们强调了疫苗接种对于防止此类可预防悲剧的重要性。
