NEWYou can now listen to Fox News articles! An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, the state's Department of Health Services announced on Thursday. The Department of Health Services said the child died in southwestern Wisconsin but did not provide a more precise location. The department said it would not release any additional details to protect the privacy of the family. The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles. "It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family," state Department of Health Services Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement. CHILD'S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE'S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton) "Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family," she continued. Measles can cause life-threatening complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The department said that while anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than 5, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications. Video Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year, reflecting the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years. Among these cases, nine people required hospitalization for severe symptoms. State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images) The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services previously told FOX News Digital that "Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles." Earlier this week, a child in New York state's Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "heartbroken" to learn of the child's death. "As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child," Hochul said in a statement. NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images) CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported four measles-associated deaths across the country this year, although state health departments have reported higher figures. In Pennsylvania, state health officials have confirmed six measles-associated deaths in 2026 and are investigating another reported death that has not yet met the state's criteria to be classified as measles-associated. The Associated Press contributed to this report. Continue

Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print A sign providing information about measles in Seminole, Texas, on April 9, 2025. Brandon Bell/Getty Images Kimberly Hayek 11/6/2026|Updated: 11/6/2026 0:00 X 1 Wisconsin health officials reported on Thursday the death of an infant tied to the ongoing measles outbreak in the southwestern part of the state, making it the first fatality of its kind since 1990. The coroner declared the immediate cause of death as measles. To protect the privacy of the family and the child, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services will not release any additional information related to the death. “It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family,” the department’s secretary, Kirsten Johnson, said in a statement. “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.” Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes. Related Stories Pennsylvania Confirms 6th Measles-Associated Death New York Reports 1st Measles-Related Death in More Than 30 Years Symptoms typically begin with fever, cough, a runny nose, and red, watery eyes, followed several days later by a rash that starts on the face and spreads downward. The disease can lead to serious complications, including pneumonia and encephalitis. As of Nov. 3, the department has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far in 2026, the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years. Across these cases, nine people have required hospitalization for severe symptoms. Reported case counts may not reflect the full extent of measles spread because not everyone who becomes ill seeks medical care or gets tested, which means cases may go unreported, according to the department. It recommends that anyone exposed to measles should stay at home. Wisconsin health officials said that the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine. Two doses are approximately 97 percent effective at preventing measles. Since Aug.1, more than 42,000 doses of MMR vaccine have been administered by healthcare providers in the state. About 95 percent of people who contracted the viral infection were unvaccinated or had an undetermined vaccination status, according to the department. Two percent had one dose of the MMR vaccine, while another 2 percent of cases had two doses of the vaccine. According to the most recent CDC data for the 2025–2026 school year, the lowest kindergarten MMR vaccination rates were recorded in Idaho (75.2 percent) and Wisconsin (85.1 percent), well below the national average of 92.4 percent. Other states with comparatively low coverage included Utah (87.2 percent), Arizona (87.4 percent), and Colorado (87.7 percent), while Alaska stood at 89.9 percent. High-coverage states such as West Virginia reached 98.9 percent. As of its Oct. 29 update, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention listed 4,852 confirmed measles cases in the United States this year and four deaths. More than half of all cases were in children and young adults, the agency said. Approximately 17 percent were children younger than 5, and 42 percent were between ages 5 and 19. Eighteen measles cases were confirmed among international travelers to the United States. We had a problem loading this article. Please enable javascript or use a different browser. New York Had Its First Measles Death in 30 Years. Here’s What to Know Cases are still surging across the country amidst dropping vaccination rates Sara Hashemi | Daily Correspondent November 4, 2026 Share Copy linkEmailSMSFacebookXRedditLinkedInBlueskyPrint Add as preferred source Measles virus particle. Science Photo Library via Getty Images A 7-month-old child in New York died of measles on Monday, marking the state’s first death from the disease in more than 30 years. Report Ad New York Governor Kathy Hochul said in a statement that she was “heartbroken,” and that the death is “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.” Last month, Hochul declared measles a statewide disaster. Measles is a highly infectious viral illness that infects the respiratory tract. Once eliminated from the United States, cases in the country have now reached the highest they’ve been in 35 years, with more than 5,000 cases counted so far. Pennsylvania is seeing the worst of it, with 140 cases counted in just the last two weeks and more than a thousand this year. These outbreaks put the United States at risk of losing its official measles elimination status, gained in 2000. “The U.S. is in the throes of the deadliest measles outbreak it has seen in decades,” said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiologist and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University, to Lauren J. Young at Scientific American at the beginning of the year. “Losing measles elimination status is an official acknowledgement that the country is on the wrong path.” This comes at a time of increased vaccine hesitancy and widespread anti-vaccine rhetoric by officials like Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In January, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) overhauled its immunization schedules for kids, dropping a number of recommended vaccines. While that decision didn’t include measles, vaccination rates for the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) combined shot in kindergartners have dropped to 92.4 percent, which is below the critical 95 percent threshold for herd immunity. Quick fact: Current immunization schedule for kids in the U.S. The CDC now recommends 11 immunizations for children, down from 17 in 2025. The six dropped from the list by January 2026 included immunizations for hepatitis A, hepatitis B, influenza, meningitis, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and rotavirus. Roughly 96 percent of people infected with measles this year were either unvaccinated or had an unknown vaccination status, according to CDC data. Jeffery Tompkins, the coroner and district attorney of Lewis County, where the child died, confirmed to Joseph Goldstein at the New York Times that the infant was not vaccinated. Children typically receive the first dose of the MMR vaccine when they are between 12 and 15 months of age, though public health authorities can recommend that a child receive a dose at 6 months if there is a community outbreak. “The MMR vaccine is the best way to prevent measles and stop outbreaks,” says Andrew D. Racine, the president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, to Melissa Jenco at AAP News. “It is safe, reliable, inexpensive and readily available. When enough people are vaccinated, the virus can’t spread throughout the community.” While most measles outbreaks still mainly happen in countries with low income or weak health infrastructure, the United States is not the only high-income country facing rising cases. Last year, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked Canada’s measles elimination status because it had 12 months of continual measles transmission. The United Kingdom is also experiencing a surge of cases. Experts blame decreasing vaccination rates for both countries. PAHO will meet from November 10 to 13, when the United States is widely expected to lose its measles elimination status. analysis.time: The measles death in New York occurred on Monday, November 1, 2026, as reported in N4. The article was published on November 4, 2026 (N1, N2, N3).
analysis.location_and_population: The event took place in New York, specifically in Lewis County, where the 7-month-old child died (N4). The article also mentions measles outbreaks across the United States, with Pennsylvania reporting 140 cases in the last two weeks and over a thousand this year (N8).
analysis.event: A 7-month-old child in New York died of measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in over 30 years (N4). The article reports that measles cases are surging across the country amidst dropping vaccination rates (N3).
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: As of the time of the report, more than 5,000 measles cases have been counted in the United States, with the highest numbers in Pennsylvania (N7, N8). The CDC notes that roughly 96 percent of people infected with measles this year were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status (N18). The outbreaks have put the U.S. at risk of losing its measles elimination status, which was achieved in 2000 (N9).
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared measles a statewide disaster last month and expressed concern over the death (N5). The CDC has revised its immunization schedules, which may have contributed to the decline in vaccination rates (N13, N14). The coroner confirmed the child was not vaccinated (N19).

analysis.brief_en: A 7-month-old child in New York died of measles on Monday, November 1, 2026, marking the state’s first measles death in over 30 years (N4). The incident occurred amid a surge in measles cases across the U.S., with more than 5,000 cases reported so far, and Pennsylvania experiencing the highest number of cases (N7, N8). The CDC notes that 96% of those infected this year were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status (N18). New York Governor Kathy Hochul called the death a 'devastating reminder' of the risks posed by declining vaccination rates and declared measles a statewide disaster last month (N5). The CDC has revised its immunization schedules, which may have contributed to the drop in MMR vaccination rates among kindergartners to 92.4%, below the 95% threshold needed for herd immunity (N13, N14). The child’s coroner confirmed they were not vaccinated (N19).

Image: NIAID via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0 6 hours ago 6 hours ago LIVE US measles cases pass 5,000 for the first time since 1991 as deaths reach eight US measles cases have passed 5,000 for the first time since 1991, at 5,182 across 45 states and Washington, D.C., and eight people have died, including a child in New York and an infant in Wisconsin. #Measles #UnitedStates #PublicHealth #CDC by ASTIG PR 6 hours ago6 hours ago Advertisements Discover more Buy Maps Learn Tagalog Look Up Facts The United States has now confirmed more measles cases in 2026 than in any year since 1991, and the outbreak has killed eight people, including an infant in Wisconsin and a child in New York, the first measles deaths in those states in decades. CDC data updated on Friday put the national total at 5,182 confirmed cases, with infections reported in 45 states and Washington, D.C. Eighteen of the cases were in international visitors. What the latest CDC count shows It is the first time the national count has passed 5,000 since the early 1990s, when a resurgence from 1989 to 1991 produced 55,000 infections and 123 deaths. The 2026 tally is already more than double the 2,289 cases recorded in all of 2025. Most cases are in people who were not vaccinated. The CDC said 2 percent of cases were among people who had received one dose of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, and another 2 percent among people who had received both recommended doses. Measure Figure Confirmed US cases in 2026 5,182 States with reported cases 45, plus Washington, D.C. Measles-associated deaths in 2026 8 Deaths by state 6 in Pennsylvania, 1 in New York, 1 in Wisconsin Deaths confirmed by the CDC so far 4, a number the agency says is subject to change Cases in all of 2025 2,289 Kindergarten MMR coverage, 2025-2026 92.4 percent Kindergarten MMR coverage, 2019-2020 95.2 percent Two states recorded their first measles deaths in decades Discover more Compare Deals Launch a Store Compare Broadband New York’s health department said on Wednesday that a child who lived in upstate New York had died with measles, the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years. A day later, Wisconsin health officials said an infant had died with measles, the first measles death in that state since 1990. Six of the eight deaths have been in Pennsylvania. The state’s outbreak began in April west of Philadelphia and has centred on Lancaster County, which has sizable Amish and Mennonite populations. By October 14, Pennsylvania had confirmed 1,222 cases, its largest outbreak in more than three decades, with at least 219 people hospitalized. The CDC has confirmed four of the eight deaths nationwide and said the figure is subject to change. Why the outbreak keeps growing Vaccination coverage has slipped below the level needed to stop measles from spreading. About 92.4 percent of kindergarteners received their MMR shots in the 2025-2026 school year, down from 95.2 percent in 2019-2020, and only 10 states reached the 95 percent threshold last year. CBS News reported that the ongoing outbreaks have put the United States at risk of losing its measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000. Measles was declared eliminated that year through high vaccination rates, and coverage has since fallen under the roughly 95 percent needed to keep outbreaks from spreading. The CDC recommends two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old before school entry. One dose is about 93 percent effective, and two doses about 97 percent effective against measles. What New York did in October New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency in October as cases climbed in underimmunized rural communities, a step that let the state test and vaccinate people faster. New York had confirmed 108 measles cases as of October 3, including seven in New York City. Why the US count matters in the Philippines Measles spreads the same way wherever vaccination coverage falls. In Cebu province, this year’s measles-rubella immunization drive reached only 21.2 percent of its target children, down from about 90 percent in 2023, provincial health officials said, pointing to vaccine misinformation. That drive ran from August 10 to September 4 and targeted children aged six months to 59 months, with vitamin A supplementation. Coverage ranged from about 55 percent in the best-performing local government units to about 10 percent in the lowest. The CDC updates its national measles figures weekly. As of Friday, the 2026 count stood at 5,182 confirmed cases and eight deaths. (Image: A colorized transmission electron micrograph of a measles virus particle. Microscopy by the CDC, colorization by NIAID, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.) CBS News reported that the ongoing outbreaks have put the United States at risk of losing its measles elimination status, which it has held since 2000. Measles was declared eliminated that year through high vaccination rates, and coverage has since fallen under the roughly 95 percent needed to keep outbreaks from spreading. The CDC recommends two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old before school entry. One dose is about 93 percent effective, and two doses about 97 percent effective against measles. What New York did in October New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency in October as cases climbed in underimmunized rural communities, a step that let the state test and vaccinate people faster. New York had confirmed 108 measles cases as of October 3, including seven in New York City. Why the US count matters in the Philippines Measles spreads the same way wherever vaccination coverage falls. In Cebu province, this year’s measles-rubella immunization drive reached only 21.2 percent of its target children, down from about 90 percent in 2023, provincial health officials said, pointing to vaccine misinformation. That drive ran from August 10 to September 4 and targeted children aged six months to 59 months, with vitamin A supplementation. Coverage ranged from about 55 percent in the best-performing local government units to about 10 percent in the lowest. The CDC updates its national measles figures weekly. As of Friday, the 2026 count stood at 5,182 confirmed cases and eight deaths. (Image: A colorized transmission electron micrograph of a measles virus particle. See Full Bio Follow: Mark Freie Mark Freie See Full Bio Follow: Nov 06, 2026, 12:15 PM CT LocalNewswccoradio Measles cases continue to climb across Minnesota, echoing a pattern seen across a number of U.S. states. The Minnesota Department of Health report earlier this week that there are now 122 confirmed cases of measles since mid-September. Todd County has seen the biggest outbreak this year, with 115 total cases, including 58 confirmed cases just in the last week due to what health officials say is a widespread lack of vaccination. 139 total cases have been reported this year in total, compared to just 26 all of last year. This marks the highest total in Minnesota since 1990, and is nearly double the highest in the last decade. The news comes as health officials reported on Thursday that an infant has died from measles in southwestern Wisconsin, marking that state's first measles-related death since 1990. Other areas in the Northeast have been hard hit as well. Lancaster County in Pennsylvania has been the epicenter of the nation's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. It's also home to the largest Amish population in the U.S. Some Amish and related Mennonite groups, with historically lower rates of vaccination, have been hit hard. Vaccination rates also declined in the general population amid the resurgence of a contagious virus considered “eliminated” from the U.S. since 2000. Pennsylvania leads the U.S. this year with over 1,350 cases. A child in rural northern New York has also died after contracting measles, marking that state’s first death from the disease in 30 years. Measles spreads easily when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, or through contaminated surfaces. “Measles is really the lion king of infectious diseases when it comes to transmission,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “No one in the United States of America who is susceptible to the measles virus, either having not been vaccinated or not having previously had it, should feel safe from measles. No one.” The U.S. is currently experiencing a resurgence of measles, with the number of confirmed measles cases reported in the U.S. in both 2025 and 2026 exceeding that of any year since 1991. The risk grows as vaccination rates decline. Vaccine hesitancy that rose across populations during the pandemic still lingers. That's eroded “herd immunity,” which occurs when enough people in an area have immunity to measles that it no longer spreads easily. Although nothing short of 100% immunity guarantees the virus won’t spread, an outbreak is considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received the required MMR shots. That’s down from 95.2% in 2019-20. See Full Bio Follow: Mark Freie Mark Freie See Full Bio Follow: Nov 06, 2026, 12:15 PM CT LocalNewswccoradio Measles cases continue to climb across Minnesota, echoing a pattern seen across a number of U.S. states. The Minnesota Department of Health report earlier this week that there are now 122 confirmed cases of measles since mid-September. Todd County has seen the biggest outbreak this year, with 115 total cases, including 58 confirmed cases just in the last week due to what health officials say is a widespread lack of vaccination. 139 total cases have been reported this year in total, compared to just 26 all of last year. This marks the highest total in Minnesota since 1990, and is nearly double the highest in the last decade. The news comes as health officials reported on Thursday that an infant has died from measles in southwestern Wisconsin, marking that state's first measles-related death since 1990. Other areas in the Northeast have been hard hit as well. Lancaster County in Pennsylvania has been the epicenter of the nation's worst measles outbreak in 35 years. It's also home to the largest Amish population in the U.S. Some Amish and related Mennonite groups, with historically lower rates of vaccination, have been hit hard. Vaccination rates also declined in the general population amid the resurgence of a contagious virus considered “eliminated” from the U.S. since 2000. Pennsylvania leads the U.S. this year with over 1,350 cases. A child in rural northern New York has also died after contracting measles, marking that state’s first death from the disease in 30 years. Measles spreads easily when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, or through contaminated surfaces. “Measles is really the lion king of infectious diseases when it comes to transmission,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “No one in the United States of America who is susceptible to the measles virus, either having not been vaccinated or not having previously had it, should feel safe from measles. No one.” The U.S. is currently experiencing a resurgence of measles, with the number of confirmed measles cases reported in the U.S. in both 2025 and 2026 exceeding that of any year since 1991. The risk grows as vaccination rates decline. Vaccine hesitancy that rose across populations during the pandemic still lingers. That's eroded “herd immunity,” which occurs when enough people in an area have immunity to measles that it no longer spreads easily. Although nothing short of 100% immunity guarantees the virus won’t spread, an outbreak is considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received the required MMR shots. That’s down from 95.2% in 2019-20. The Minnesota Department of Health reported 122 confirmed measles cases since mid-September, and Todd County has seen 115 total cases, including 58 confirmed in the last week. This outbreak is part of a broader resurgence of measles in the U.S., with Pennsylvania reporting over 1,350 cases this year, the highest in decades. Health officials have noted that an infant in Wisconsin and a child in New York have died from measles, marking the first deaths in those states since 1990. The outbreak is attributed to widespread vaccine hesitancy and declining vaccination rates, which have eroded herd immunity. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners received the required MMR shots in 2025-26, down from 95.2% in 2019-20. The situation remains under investigation, with a focus on addressing vaccination gaps and preventing further spread.
news.content_zh: 明尼苏达州目前正在发生 麻疹 暴发,其中托德县的病例数量最多。自 9 月中旬以来,明尼苏达州卫生部报告了 122 例 麻疹 确诊病例,托德县累计确诊 115 例,其中上周确诊 58 例。此次 麻疹 是 麻疹 在美国更广泛复苏的一部分,宾夕法尼亚州今年报告了超过 1,350 例病例,为几十年来最高。卫生官员指出,威斯康星州的一名婴儿和纽约州的一名儿童死于 麻疹,这是这些州自 1990 年以来首次死亡。暴发 的原因是人们对 疫苗 的普遍犹豫和 疫苗接种 发病率的下降,从而削弱了群体免疫力。美国疾病控制与预防中心报告称,2025-26 年,92.4% 的美国幼儿园儿童接种了所需的 MMR 疫苗,低于 2019-20 年的 95.2%。目前情况仍在调查中,重点是解决 疫苗接种 漏洞并防止进一步传播。

Over the Air & Streaming KSMU - Over the Air & Streaming Newsletters News Measles case confirmed in Christian County KSMU | By Michele Skalicky Published November 5, 2026 at 6:51 PM CST Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email CDC The measles virus. The person infected was exposed to a confirmed case in another county. A case of measles has been reported to the Christian County Health Department. According to the department, a county resident tested positive after being exposed to a reported case in another county. Those who have been exposed are being contacted and asked to watch for symptoms. There have been three cases reported in Greene County this year. Christian County Health Administrator Aaron Winslow said in a statement that measles can no longer be viewed as "a disease of faraway places or the distant past." He said this case will not lead to a community outbreak due to efforts of state and public health officials, but he said they may not be so lucky next time. He said the best way to prevent an outbreak is to achieve community immunity through vaccination. "The best way to prevent getting sick is to be immunized with two doses of a measles-containing vaccine, which is primarily administered as the combination measles-mumps-rubella or MMR vaccine," according to the health department. "Two doses of the MMR vaccine provide 97 percent protection from measles infections." The kindergarten vaccination rate for MMR in Christian County for the 2025-2026 school year was 84.2%. Measles is a highly contagious viral illness – one person with the illness can easily pass it on to 9 out of 10 people around them who are unvaccinated or don’t have natural immunity. Symptoms start around two weeks from exposure and typically begin with fever, cough, runny nose and red and watery eyes. Tiny white spots may appear in the mouth two to three days after symptoms start. A rash begins three to five days after the first symptoms. Anyone who suspects they might have measles should call their healthcare provider. Measles can cause severe health complications, including pneumonia, encephalitis (inflammation of the brain) and death, according to the health department. The virus can be transmitted by direct contact with infectious droplets or by airborne spread when an infected person breathes, coughs or sneezes. The virus can remain infectious in the air and on surfaces for up to 2 hours after an infected person leaves an area. She enjoys working on both the announcing side and in news and has been the recipient of statewide and national awards for news reporting. She likes to tell stories that make a difference. Michele enjoys outdoor activities, including hiking, camping and leisurely kayaking. See stories by Michele Skalicky

Associated Press November 5, 2026 • Southwest Region An undated electron microscope image provided by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows a measles virus particle. (Source: Cynthia Goldsmith / CDC via AP, File) MADISON, Wis. (AP) — An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state’s first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Nov. 5. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services did not specify where the death happened or provide any additional details to protect the privacy of the family. The coroner listed the cause of death as measles, state health officials said. “My heart is broken for the family,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the state health department. “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease.” The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed four measles-associated deaths in the U.S. in 2026, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. In Pennsylvania alone, health officials have reported five deaths in 2026 and are investigating a possible sixth. As of Nov. 5, Wisconsin reported 431 cases of measles, all but three in unvaccinated people. Nine people had been hospitalized. ✓ Thanks for sharing! More... Notifications

Associated Press November 5, 2026 • Southwest Region An undated electron microscope image provided by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on Feb. 4, 2015, shows a measles virus particle. (Source: Cynthia Goldsmith / CDC via AP, File) MADISON, Wis. (AP) — An infant in southwestern Wisconsin has died after contracting measles, the state’s first death from the disease in 36 years, state officials announced Nov. 5. The Wisconsin Department of Health Services did not specify where the death happened or provide any additional details to protect the privacy of the family. The coroner listed the cause of death as measles, state health officials said. “My heart is broken for the family,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the state health department. “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease.” The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed four measles-associated deaths in the U.S. in 2026, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. In Pennsylvania alone, health officials have reported five deaths in 2026 and are investigating a possible sixth. As of Nov. 5, Wisconsin reported 431 cases of measles, all but three in unvaccinated people. Nine people had been hospitalized. ✓ Thanks for sharing! More... Notifications

(AP Photo/Jessie Wardarski) EPHRATA, Pa. (AP) — Amish and Mennonite shoppers in conservative dress mingled with shoppers from the wider public on a recent Friday at a vast outdoor market here, where vendors sold colorful pumpkins and mums, fry pies and squash, sports jerseys and Barbie accessories. Such interactions are common in Lancaster County in central Pennsylvania, home to the largest Amish population in the U.S. — and the epicenter of the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 35 years. While they avoid many types of civic engagement for religious reasons, the Amish — like many other groups vulnerable to measles across the nation — are not truly separate. “We are all interconnected,” said Dr. Diego Hijano of St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. Robust vaccination rates once protected Americans much better. But rates among the general public are now falling, and rates have long been low among the Amish, creating the perfect conditions for the contagious virus — officially considered “eliminated” from the U.S. since 2000 — to spread here and beyond. Pennsylvania has the most U.S. cases, with over 1,350 this year, more than a third in Lancaster County alone, according to state figures. That’s a big undercount, community leaders say, since many people with measles never see a doctor. The state has recorded three measles-associated deaths in Lancaster and two in other counties. In Amish Country, a Measles Surge Poses Questions About Vaccine Acceptance The outbreak has especially hit the “Plain communities” of Amish and conservative Mennonites — so named for their modest dress and limited use of technology. Vaccination rates, and attitudes about vaccines, range widely. But overall, they are less likely to be vaccinated than the general population, due more to culture and habit than doctrine. Many are now showing a new openness to vaccines, while members of the general public are also taking extra precautions. All of this has underscored the interconnectedness of Plain and wider “English” populations. The Plain People avoid such areas of civic participation as holding public office. Still, they regularly shop and do business with their neighbors in this growing county of half a million people, where an urban core is ringed by suburban subdivisions abutting Amish farms. “There’s no way to imagine that this is going to be an isolated community,” said Dr. Anne-Marie Derrico, chief medical officer at the nonprofit Union Community Care. It has clinics in the city of Lancaster and outlying towns, along with a mobile unit operating a “Plain Healthy” outreach to the Amish and to Mennonites. “We have Plain patients coming to the city, we have patients in the city who don’t vaccinate, who are going to school, going to other programs with other children,” Derrico said. Pennsylvania’s measles rates have declined from their September peak, but some doctors expect them to rise as winter brings more indoor gatherings. While most cases are mild, measles can cause serious and even fatal complications, such as pneumonia and encephalitis. Union has held small-scale vaccine clinics to reach Plain populations, resulting in about 450 measles shots. “That’s hopefully made a significant impact,” Derrico said. Union’s clinics are also offering vaccinations for infants earlier than normally scheduled, as health experts advise in areas experiencing measles outbreaks. Lauren and Mason Spence brought their 10-month-old son, Bowen, to a clinic recently to get his first dose of the MMR vaccine, short for measles, mumps and rubella. The “English” family frequently goes to public places, including farmers markets. “It’s scary,” Lauren Spence said. “It’s spreading quick.” Vaccine Views Vary Among Plain People Attitudes toward vaccines in Plain communities have alternately warmed and cooled over time — most recently cooling in reaction to strict COVID-19 public health measures, according to community leaders and scholars. The measles outbreak is prompting many to accept the shots while reinforcing vaccine skepticism in others. One Amish farmer, Ephraim Zook, still opposes vaccines even after he and his wife nursed their young twins through the illness. “We just felt that measles is a natural thing,” he said. A Mennonite market vendor said his largely vaccinated community has had no infections. One Plain farmer said he got vaccinated after his adult siblings began getting measles. With vegetables to harvest and tobacco leaves to pick, “I thought, if I get it, I’m going to be done,” he said. Most interviewed by the AP asked not to use their names, in keeping with Plain traditions of not calling attention to themselves. Those who avoid vaccines usually aren’t driven by ideology, community leaders and experts say. “The overwhelming reason had nothing to do with being against vaccinations,” said Allen Hoover, an Old Order Mennonite and former administrator of the Parochial Medical Center in the town of New Holland. “It was simply, ‘Well, we never did before, and we came through all right.’” Hoover said the most effective strategy for medical workers is to encourage vaccination — not to push it aggressively. It takes time for outside professionals to build trust in Plain communities, he said. About how long? “Twenty years,” he said. One cluster of Amish schools and individuals in New York is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to require their state to allow exemptions to school vaccine requirements on religious grounds, as Pennsylvania and most states do. But the wider Amish leadership hasn’t presented this as a religious issue, according to Steve Nolt, director of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College in Lancaster County. “There’s nothing in Amish theology or historic documents that you can find that specifically addresses or is opposed to immunization,” he said. About 45,000 Amish and 6,000 Old Order Mennonites live in and around Lancaster County, according to the Young Center. Many rely on traditional remedies and visit doctors infrequently, Nolt said. This year’s outbreak follows ones in 2025 in Mennonite communities in Texas and elsewhere across North America. Contagious Virus a Rising Threat to Everyone Measles spreads easily when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, or through contaminated surfaces. “Measles is really the lion king of infectious diseases when it comes to transmission,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “No one in the United States of America who is susceptible to the measles virus, either having not been vaccinated or not having previously had it, should feel safe from measles. No one.” The risk grows as vaccination rates decline. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received the required MMR shots. That’s down from 95.2% in 2019-20. “Though Plain communities are an easy and recognizable target, declining childhood vaccination rates in our county are not limited to the Amish,” wrote Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, in a recent commentary. “Kindergarten vaccination rates have declined in every central Pennsylvania county since 2020.” A 2022 survey by the center found the vast majority of Mennonite families reported having their children vaccinated, compared to about 3 in 10 Amish families. Yost urged the public not to blame the Amish, or any group, for the outbreak. “Every one of us is susceptible to misinformation and confusing messages,” he wrote. Vaccine hesitancy that rose across populations during the pandemic still lingers. That’s eroded “herd immunity,” which occurs when enough people in an area have immunity to measles that it no longer spreads easily. Although nothing short of 100% immunity guarantees the virus won’t spread, an outbreak is considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate. Pennsylvania’s kindergarten MMR vaccination rate fell to 93.2% last year. Lancaster County’s rate is 88%, with rates lower in the county’s religious and other private schools than in public schools, according to an AP review of state data. Across the county and state, the percentage of students receiving religious or philosophical exemptions from at least one required vaccination has risen significantly. Nolt said some anti-vaccine groups targeted the Amish with their messaging. In 2021, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who helped lead the anti-vaccine movement for years, spoke at a Lancaster County fair, alleging the government was trying to force the Amish to vaccinate. Now U.S. health secretary, Kennedy recently sparred with Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, over the extent of the outbreak. Further controversy ensued when the county coroner attributed the death of a measles-infected infant to a ruptured spleen, not the disease itself. After a Decline in Trust, Some Minds Are Changing Lancaster County Commissioner Alice Yoder said public officials should unite behind the message that the vaccine is safe and effective and should encourage people to get it. That approach succeeded during Pennsylvania’s last measles outbreak in 1991. “There were lines of people in the Plain community that would come and get vaccinated,” she said. Dr. D. Holmes Morton, who founded the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Mifflin County — which treats Plain patients with genetic diseases — said the same is happening now. “We are having more success at having vaccine days,” he said. Ultimately, this will keep everyone safer, said Hijano of St. Jude. Getting the shot is “an act of love to your community,” he said. “You will get protected yourself. But in truth, you are actually protecting everyone around you.” ___ Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. (AP Photo/Jessie Wardarski) EPHRATA, Pa. (AP) — Amish and Mennonite shoppers in conservative dress mingled with shoppers from the wider public on a recent Friday at a vast outdoor market here, where vendors sold colorful pumpkins and mums, fry pies and squash, sports jerseys and Barbie accessories. Such interactions are common in Lancaster County in central Pennsylvania, home to the largest Amish population in the U.S. — and the epicenter of the nation’s worst measles outbreak in 35 years. While they avoid many types of civic engagement for religious reasons, the Amish — like many other groups vulnerable to measles across the nation — are not truly separate. “We are all interconnected,” said Dr. Diego Hijano of St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital. Robust vaccination rates once protected Americans much better. But rates among the general public are now falling, and rates have long been low among the Amish, creating the perfect conditions for the contagious virus — officially considered “eliminated” from the U.S. since 2000 — to spread here and beyond. Pennsylvania has the most U.S. cases, with over 1,350 this year, more than a third in Lancaster County alone, according to state figures. That’s a big undercount, community leaders say, since many people with measles never see a doctor. The state has recorded three measles-associated deaths in Lancaster and two in other counties. In Amish Country, a Measles Surge Poses Questions About Vaccine Acceptance The outbreak has especially hit the “Plain communities” of Amish and conservative Mennonites — so named for their modest dress and limited use of technology. Vaccination rates, and attitudes about vaccines, range widely. But overall, they are less likely to be vaccinated than the general population, due more to culture and habit than doctrine. Many are now showing a new openness to vaccines, while members of the general public are also taking extra precautions. All of this has underscored the interconnectedness of Plain and wider “English” populations. The Plain People avoid such areas of civic participation as holding public office. Still, they regularly shop and do business with their neighbors in this growing county of half a million people, where an urban core is ringed by suburban subdivisions abutting Amish farms. “There’s no way to imagine that this is going to be an isolated community,” said Dr. Anne-Marie Derrico, chief medical officer at the nonprofit Union Community Care. It has clinics in the city of Lancaster and outlying towns, along with a mobile unit operating a “Plain Healthy” outreach to the Amish and to Mennonites. “We have Plain patients coming to the city, we have patients in the city who don’t vaccinate, who are going to school, going to other programs with other children,” Derrico said. Pennsylvania’s measles rates have declined from their September peak, but some doctors expect them to rise as winter brings more indoor gatherings. While most cases are mild, measles can cause serious and even fatal complications, such as pneumonia and encephalitis. Union has held small-scale vaccine clinics to reach Plain populations, resulting in about 450 measles shots. “That’s hopefully made a significant impact,” Derrico said. Union’s clinics are also offering vaccinations for infants earlier than normally scheduled, as health experts advise in areas experiencing measles outbreaks. Lauren and Mason Spence brought their 10-month-old son, Bowen, to a clinic recently to get his first dose of the MMR vaccine, short for measles, mumps and rubella. The “English” family frequently goes to public places, including farmers markets. “It’s scary,” Lauren Spence said. “It’s spreading quick.” Vaccine Views Vary Among Plain People Attitudes toward vaccines in Plain communities have alternately warmed and cooled over time — most recently cooling in reaction to strict COVID-19 public health measures, according to community leaders and scholars. The measles outbreak is prompting many to accept the shots while reinforcing vaccine skepticism in others. One Amish farmer, Ephraim Zook, still opposes vaccines even after he and his wife nursed their young twins through the illness. “We just felt that measles is a natural thing,” he said. A Mennonite market vendor said his largely vaccinated community has had no infections. One Plain farmer said he got vaccinated after his adult siblings began getting measles. With vegetables to harvest and tobacco leaves to pick, “I thought, if I get it, I’m going to be done,” he said. Most interviewed by the AP asked not to use their names, in keeping with Plain traditions of not calling attention to themselves. Those who avoid vaccines usually aren’t driven by ideology, community leaders and experts say. “The overwhelming reason had nothing to do with being against vaccinations,” said Allen Hoover, an Old Order Mennonite and former administrator of the Parochial Medical Center in the town of New Holland. “It was simply, ‘Well, we never did before, and we came through all right.’” Hoover said the most effective strategy for medical workers is to encourage vaccination — not to push it aggressively. It takes time for outside professionals to build trust in Plain communities, he said. About how long? “Twenty years,” he said. One cluster of Amish schools and individuals in New York is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to require their state to allow exemptions to school vaccine requirements on religious grounds, as Pennsylvania and most states do. But the wider Amish leadership hasn’t presented this as a religious issue, according to Steve Nolt, director of the Young Center for Anabaptist and Pietist Studies at Elizabethtown College in Lancaster County. “There’s nothing in Amish theology or historic documents that you can find that specifically addresses or is opposed to immunization,” he said. About 45,000 Amish and 6,000 Old Order Mennonites live in and around Lancaster County, according to the Young Center. Many rely on traditional remedies and visit doctors infrequently, Nolt said. This year’s outbreak follows ones in 2025 in Mennonite communities in Texas and elsewhere across North America. Contagious Virus a Rising Threat to Everyone Measles spreads easily when people who have it breathe, cough or sneeze, or through contaminated surfaces. “Measles is really the lion king of infectious diseases when it comes to transmission,” said Michael Osterholm, who directs the University of Minnesota’s Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy. “No one in the United States of America who is susceptible to the measles virus, either having not been vaccinated or not having previously had it, should feel safe from measles. No one.” The risk grows as vaccination rates decline. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 92.4% of U.S. kindergarteners in 2025-26 received the required MMR shots. That’s down from 95.2% in 2019-20. “Though Plain communities are an easy and recognizable target, declining childhood vaccination rates in our county are not limited to the Amish,” wrote Berwood Yost, director of the Center for Opinion Research at Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster, in a recent commentary. “Kindergarten vaccination rates have declined in every central Pennsylvania county since 2020.” A 2022 survey by the center found the vast majority of Mennonite families reported having their children vaccinated, compared to about 3 in 10 Amish families. Yost urged the public not to blame the Amish, or any group, for the outbreak. “Every one of us is susceptible to misinformation and confusing messages,” he wrote. Vaccine hesitancy that rose across populations during the pandemic still lingers. That’s eroded “herd immunity,” which occurs when enough people in an area have immunity to measles that it no longer spreads easily. Although nothing short of 100% immunity guarantees the virus won’t spread, an outbreak is considered unlikely if a community has a 95% MMR rate. Pennsylvania’s kindergarten MMR vaccination rate fell to 93.2% last year. Lancaster County’s rate is 88%, with rates lower in the county’s religious and other private schools than in public schools, according to an AP review of state data. Across the county and state, the percentage of students receiving religious or philosophical exemptions from at least one required vaccination has risen significantly. Nolt said some anti-vaccine groups targeted the Amish with their messaging. In 2021, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who helped lead the anti-vaccine movement for years, spoke at a Lancaster County fair, alleging the government was trying to force the Amish to vaccinate. Now U.S. health secretary, Kennedy recently sparred with Pennsylvania’s Democratic governor, Josh Shapiro, over the extent of the outbreak. Further controversy ensued when the county coroner attributed the death of a measles-infected infant to a ruptured spleen, not the disease itself. After a Decline in Trust, Some Minds Are Changing Lancaster County Commissioner Alice Yoder said public officials should unite behind the message that the vaccine is safe and effective and should encourage people to get it. That approach succeeded during Pennsylvania’s last measles outbreak in 1991. “There were lines of people in the Plain community that would come and get vaccinated,” she said. Dr. D. Holmes Morton, who founded the Central Pennsylvania Clinic in Mifflin County — which treats Plain patients with genetic diseases — said the same is happening now. “We are having more success at having vaccine days,” he said. Ultimately, this will keep everyone safer, said Hijano of St. Jude. Getting the shot is “an act of love to your community,” he said. “You will get protected yourself. But in truth, you are actually protecting everyone around you.” ___ Associated Press religion coverage receives support through the AP’s collaboration with The Conversation US, with funding from Lilly Endowment Inc. analysis.brief_en: A historic measles outbreak has hit Pennsylvania Amish Country, with over 1,350 cases reported in the state this year, more than a third in Lancaster County alone. news.source_body_en: A historic measles outbreak has hit Pennsylvania Amish Country, with over 1,350 cases reported in the state this year, more than a third in Lancaster County alone. The outbreak has prompted some members of the Amish and Mennonite communities to show openness to vaccines, while others remain skeptical. The virus, officially considered 'eliminated' in the U.S. since 2000, is spreading due to low vaccination rates among the Amish and declining rates in the general public. Measles can cause serious complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis. Health officials are conducting outreach efforts, including mobile clinics and small-scale vaccine clinics, to increase vaccination rates among the Amish and Mennonite communities. These efforts have resulted in about 450 measles shots. The state has recorded a decline in measles rates from their September peak, but some doctors expect them to rise as winter approaches. The outbreak has underscored the interconnectedness of Plain and wider 'English' populations, as many Amish and Mennonites regularly interact with the general public through activities like shopping and attending farmers markets. While most cases are mild, the outbreak has led to a surge in vaccine acceptance among some Plain community members, though others still resist due to cultural and habitual reasons rather than religious doctrine. The situation highlights the need for continued efforts to build trust and improve vaccination rates in these communities.
news.content_zh: 历史性的 麻疹 暴发 袭击了宾夕法尼亚州阿米什县,今年该州报告了超过 1,350 起病例,仅兰开斯特县就有超过三分之一。暴发 促使阿米什和门诺派社区的一些成员对 疫苗 表现出开放态度,而其他人仍然持怀疑态度。自 2000 年以来,该病毒在美国被官方认为已“消灭”,但由于阿米什人中 疫苗接种 感染率较低以及普通公众感染率不断下降,该病毒正在传播。麻疹可引起肺炎、脑炎等严重并发症。卫生官员正在开展外展工作,包括设立流动诊所和小型 疫苗 诊所,以提高阿米什人和门诺派社区的 疫苗接种 发病率。这些努力已产生约 450 个 麻疹 镜头。该州的 麻疹 发病率较 9 月份的峰值有所下降,但一些医生预计,随着冬季的临近,麻疹 发病率会上升。暴发 强调了平原和更广泛的“英国”人口之间的相互联系,因为许多阿米什人和门诺派教徒定期通过购物和参加农贸市场等活动与公众互动。虽然大多数情况都很轻微,但 暴发 导致一些平原社区成员对 疫苗 的接受度激增,尽管其他人仍然由于文化和习惯原因而不是宗教教义而抵制。这种情况凸显了需要继续努力在这些社区建立信任并提高 疫苗接种 率。

news.content: Wellness What parents need to know as measles outbreaks spread across the US 1:03 New measles death in Wisconsin New measles death in Wisconsin By Yi-Jin Yu November 06, 2026, 10:24 PM More measles cases are being reported across the U.S., and eight people have died so far, including an infant in Wisconsin , the first measles-related death in the state since 1990, according to health officials. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says there have been nearly 5,200 measles cases across 45 states and Washington, D.C., so far this year, as more have decided to opt out of vaccination. "I'm extremely concerned, and the reason for that is there's no indication that these outbreaks will be slowing down at this point," Dr. Andrew Handel, a pediatric infectious diseases physician at Stony Brook Children's Hospital in Stony Brook, New York, told ABC News. As the measles virus continues to spread, here's what parents should know about the disease. What is measles? Measles is a highly contagious virus that can cause acute respiratory illness, according to the CDC . It is more contagious that other respiratory viruses, such as the common cold, the flu or COVID. "It is the most contagious infection that we know of," Handel said. "The estimate is that for every person who has measles, they can infect up to 18 people who are unvaccinated with it." The measles virus in an image from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention website. CDC Measles is spread through the air when someone infected with the virus exhales or coughs. People can also become infected after breathing in contaminated air or by touching an infected surface and then touching their eyes, noses or mouths, the CDC states. "For measles, it spreads through airborne means, which means that once [an infected person breathes] it out, it actually stays circulating in the air for up to two hours after they leave that room," Handel explained. "If someone goes to their doctor to be checked for measles, and they don't recognize that they have measles, and then they walk out of the room, someone who comes in an hour and a half later can become infected with measles." What are the symptoms of measles? The CDC notes that measles can initially look like other respiratory infections, with symptoms including a cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis (red, watery eyes), or a high fever, which can increase to more than 104 degrees Fahrenheit. The most recognizable symptom of measles is a rash that typically starts at the head and moves down the body. "People break out into the rash, which starts as red, dark circles that usually start right at the hairline and work their way down the body," Handel said. "As it works its way down, you see the red circles, the red dots further down. But the place where it started -- so, on the face -- the redness will start to come together, so it'll look like a sheet of redness, and it, again, starts from the head and works its way down, which is very particular." Related Articles Measles cases surpass 5,000 in the US with infections confirmed in 45 states: CDC "We also see something called Koplik spots, which are usually whitish, bluish dots that can appear on the inside of the cheek," Handel added. "Those tend to come up a couple days before the rash, so it can help us to make the diagnosis a bit earlier." Measles symptoms typically begin seven to 14 days after initial contact with the virus, according to the CDC. What are the complications of measles? A common misconception about measles, as the CDC notes, is that infection with the virus isn't severe. The CDC and Handel both stress that measles infections can give rise to serious complications , from short-term issues like diarrhea and ear infections, to serious to life-threatening long-term problems and death. "Many children, many people can go on and have complications ... that can include severe pneumonias, dehydration, and also acute brain infections, where suddenly, you can have seizures," Handel said. He continued, "You can have changes in behavior. You can develop meningitis where there's neck pain and headache because the measles infection [has] infiltrated into the spinal fluid. There are some children who, especially if they're infected before they turn 1 year old, in particular, can develop a neurologic progressive disease [called subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE,] that ultimately results in death up to 10 years later. And so, there are some really scary outcomes from it." Related Articles As measles continues to spread, health officials are seeing vaccine interest rise How can measles be prevented? According to the CDC, the best way to protect against measles is with the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine , or MMR, which can be administered to children starting at 12 months old. Children who receive a first dose of the MMR vaccine then need to get a second dose when they are between 4 and 6 years old. "The only way to prevent infections when there is an ongoing national outbreak at levels that we haven't seen in decades is to get the MMR vaccine," Handel said. "It is safe, it is effective, and it's the best thing we can do again to stop this outbreak and get the country back to the rates of measles infections that we'd previously seen." Not everyone may be able to get an MMR vaccine, such as children with cancer, those who are pregnant, and people who have compromised immune systems, so it is important to discuss your children's and family's eligibility and concerns with a medical provider. OffOn Stream on Measles cases surpass 5,000 in the US with infections confirmed in 45 states: CDC Eight people have died from measles this year. ByMary Kekatos November 6, 2026, 10:13 AM Share Follow ABC News on Google Measles cases in the United States have surpassed 5,000 this year, according to newly updated data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). At least 5,182 cases have been confirmed, with cases reported in 45 states and Washington, D.C. Eighteen cases have been among international visitors to the U.S., according to the CDC. Eight measles-associated deaths have been confirmed so far in 2026: six in Pennsylvania, one in New York and one in Wisconsin. Related New map shows how to spot the measles risk level in your ZIP code Three of those deaths were confirmed by state health officials this week. On Wednesday, the New York State Department of Health reported the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years, a child who lived in upstate New York. Another death was confirmed on Wednesday in Pennsylvania among an unvaccinated resident of Jefferson County, located in the northwestern part of the state. On Thursday, Wisconsin health officials said an infant died with measles, the first death in the state since 1990. Undated electron microscope image provided by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, shows a measles virus particle. Cynthia Goldsmith/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention via AP The CDC has confirmed four of the eight deaths so far, but said the number is "subject to change." Popular Reads Thomas Markle Sr. arrested, charged with possession of child pornography 9 hours ago 4 Colorado officers shot, 1 fatally, after gunfight with suspect: Police 10 hours ago US attorney tasked with leading probe into Trump's foes resigns from DOJ 9 hours ago States with confirmed cases include Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin and Wyoming. About 96% of cases are among people who are unvaccinated or whose vaccination status is unknown, according to data from the federal health agency. Meanwhile, 2% of cases are among those who have received just one dose of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine and 2% of cases are among those who received the recommended two doses, according to the CDC. Related How hospitals, clinics in Pennsylvania are responding to the measles outbreak A plurality of cases has been recorded among those aged 5 to 19. At least 11% of cases have resulted in hospitalization, including more than 1 in 10 children under 5 years old. The CDC currently recommends that people receive two doses of the MMR vaccine, the first at ages 12 to 15 months and the second between 4 and 6 years old before school entry. One dose is 93% effective, and two doses are 97% effective against measles, the CDC says. However, CDC data shows vaccination rates have been lagging in recent years. During the 2025-26 school year, 92.4% of kindergartners received the MMR vaccine, according to data. This is lower than the 95.2% seen in the 2019-20 school year, prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. ABC News' Youri Benadjaoud contributed to this report. supplementary_news.excerpt: Ohio has nearly six times more measles cases in 2026 than last year in the latest update from the Ohio Department of Health. Where it's spreading.

supplementary_news.content_title: Ohio measles cases up nearly 600% this year, 25 counties have 2026 cases
supplementary_news.content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Boats Grocery Shopping Holidays OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Money Essentials WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services HEALTHCARE Ohio Department of Health Add Topic Ohio measles cases up nearly 600% this year, 25 counties have 2026 cases Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Nov. 6, 2026, 10:49 a.m. ET Hear this story Ohio has reported 310 measles cases in 25 counties so far in 2026, a nearly six-fold increase from all of 2025. Nationwide, measles cases have surpassed 4,700, reaching the highest annual total in 35 years. Health officials state the vast majority of cases are among unvaccinated individuals and urge vaccination as the best protection. Measles cases surged in one Ohio county as another joined the list as the state's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. The state added 14 new cases in the past week, a 61% decrease from the 36 new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 310 cases in 25 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Nov. 5. That number is nearly six times (588.9%) more than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Ashland County in north central Ohio reported seven new cases in the latest update, bringing its total this year to eight. And Mercer County in western Ohio joined the list with four reported measles cases. Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing in recent weeks: 296 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 29 260 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 22 252 cases in 23 counties on Oct. 15 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Last week, Pike County reported 20 new cases, with Van Wert County in western Ohio joining the list the week before. Also, Akron Children's Hospital announced a possible measles exposure on Oct. 20 at its main hospital building. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Oct. 30 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 5,051 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 8 (seven new cases) Ashtabula: 47 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 54 Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 Holmes: 10 Knox: 5 Medina: 27 Meigs: 4 Mercer: 4 (four new cases; first time on list) Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 Ottawa: 1 Pike: 23 (one new case) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 13 (two new cases) Tuscarawas: 13 Van Wert: 3 Vinton: 1 Wayne: 45 Wood: 1 The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least five people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 30, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. Featured Weekly Ad

supplementary_news.content_title: Measles Can Cause Fatal Brain Disease Years After Recovery: Study
supplementary_news.content: Philippines: Measles is not merely a rash-producing illness; it can cause serious complications even years after apparent recovery. A rare but almost invariably fatal neurological condition, subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) , can develop years after measles infection . A new report published in Emerging Infectious Diseases highlights this delayed complication, highlighting the importance of measles prevention through vaccination . The study, led by Maela P. Palisoc of the National Children’s Hospital, Quezon City, and the College of Medicine, San Beda University, Manila, Philippines, and colleagues, reviewed children diagnosed with SSPE over 16 years. The researchers warned that additional cases linked to the country's 2018–2019 measles outbreak could emerge in the coming years because of the long interval between infection and neurological symptoms. SSPE is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by persistent infection of the central nervous system with a defective measles virus. It typically develops several years after measles infection, particularly when infection occurs during early childhood, and is almost always fatal. For the study, researchers retrospectively examined medical records of 20 children admitted with SSPE to the National Children’s Hospital between January 2007 and December 2022. They assessed clinical characteristics, vaccination history, reported measles infection, and the estimated timing of infection in relation to national measles outbreaks. The study findings revealed the following: Recent increase in admissions: Eight of the 20 children (40%) were admitted during 2020–2022, while five (25%) were admitted in 2022 alone. Cases linked to the latest outbreak: Four children had estimated measles infection dates corresponding to the 2018–2019 outbreak. All were admitted between 2020 and 2022, approximately 2.1–3.5 years after infection. Early childhood infection: The median age at reported measles illness was 0.7 years, while the median age at hospital admission was 6.2 years. Ten of the 19 children with an estimable age at infection had contracted measles before nine months of age. Incomplete measles history: A history of measles was reported in 15 children (75%), was unknown in four (20%), and was absent in one (5%). Vaccination history: Seventeen children (85%) had reportedly received at least one measles-containing vaccine, although 11 (55%) had received only one dose. Vaccination histories were based on parental or guardian recall and were not consistently verified against records. Declining measles vaccine coverage in the Philippines may have increased susceptibility to infection, with first-dose coverage falling to 64% in 2021 amid repeated outbreaks. The researchers recommended cerebrospinal fluid measles antibody testing in children with progressive neurological deterioration and myoclonus, even without a reported history of measles, to avoid missing SSPE diagnoses. The study was limited by its small, single-center sample, lack of population-level data, and reliance on recalled histories. The researchers emphasized strengthening SSPE surveillance and sustaining two-dose measles vaccination coverage to prevent future cases. Reference: Palisoc MP, Ramones MS, Jamora RDG. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis after measles outbreaks, the Philippines, 2007–2022. Emerg Infect Dis. 2026 Nov [date cited]. https://doi.org/10.3201/eid3211.261395
