supplementary_news.content_title: Ohio measles cases up nearly 600% this year, 25 counties have 2026 cases
supplementary_news.content: News Sports Business Life & Events Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTHCARE Ohio measles cases up nearly 600% this year, 25 counties have 2026 cases Chad Murphy James Powel Mary Walrath-Holdridge USA TODAY NETWORK Nov. 6, 2026, 10:49 a.m. ET Ohio has reported 310 measles cases in 25 counties so far in 2026, a nearly six-fold increase from all of 2025. Nationwide, measles cases have surpassed 4,700, reaching the highest annual total in 35 years. Health officials state the vast majority of cases are among unvaccinated individuals and urge vaccination as the best protection. Measles cases surged in one Ohio county as another joined the list as the state's third measles outbreak of 2026 continues. The state added 14 new cases in the past week, a 61% decrease from the 36 new cases reported the week before, the Ohio Department of Health reports. ODH is reporting 310 cases in 25 counties so far this year, according to its summary of infectious diseases dashboard, updated Nov. 5. That number is nearly six times (588.9%) more than the 45 cases reported in all of 2025. Ashland County in north central Ohio reported seven new cases in the latest update, bringing its total this year to eight. And Mercer County in western Ohio joined the list with four reported measles cases. Total cases in Ohio this year have continued climbing in recent weeks: 296 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 29 260 cases in 24 counties on Oct. 22 252 cases in 23 counties on Oct. 15 228 cases in 21 counties on Oct. 8 206 cases in 20 counties on Oct. 1 196 cases in 16 counties on Sept. 24 180 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 17 133 cases in 15 counties on Sept. 10 122 cases in 14 counties on Sept. 3 107 cases in 12 counties on Aug. 27 99 cases in 12 counties Aug. 20 69 cases in 11 counties on Aug. 13 45 cases in 10 counties on Aug. 6. Last week, Pike County reported 20 new cases, with Van Wert County in western Ohio joining the list the week before. Also, Akron Children's Hospital announced a possible measles exposure on Oct. 20 at its main hospital building. The vast majority of cases in Ohio are among unvaccinated individuals, per ODH. “It’s unfortunate that these outbreaks have become more common in Ohio over the past few years, because this disease is preventable,” Dr. Bruce Vanderhoff, ODH director, said a July 30 statement. “This serves to emphasize the importance of being fully vaccinated. I strongly encourage you to protect yourselves and your children by getting vaccinated.” Measles cases nationwide have hit a 35-year high for a disease once declared eradicated in the United States. Data released Oct. 30 by the Johns Hopkins University shows 5,051 measles cases have been reported nationwide so far this year, surpassing the 2,286 infections recorded during all of 2025 and marking the highest annual total since 1991. Measles growing in Ohio. These counties report cases in 2026 Ohio counties reporting measles cases since Jan. 1, 2026, include: Ashland: 8 (seven new cases) Ashtabula: 47 Cuyahoga: 3 Franklin: 8 Gallia: 3 Geauga: 54 Hancock: 1 Harrison: 18 Holmes: 10 Knox: 5 Medina: 27 Meigs: 4 Mercer: 4 (four new cases; first time on list) Morgan: 3 Morrow: 13 Ottawa: 1 Pike: 23 (one new case) Portage: 1 Stark: 1 Trumbull: 13 (two new cases) Tuscarawas: 13 Van Wert: 3 Vinton: 1 Wayne: 45 Wood: 1 The case count for the year reflects previous outbreaks in Cuyahoga County in January and Franklin County in February. The ages of those with confirmed cases range from 15 months to 20 years old, according to various health departments. Measles cases have been growing in Ohio over the past several years, with one case in 2023, seven in 2024 and 45 cases in 2025. Pennsylvania reports measles deaths At least five people this year have died from measles in Pennsylvania as of Sept. 30, 2026, according to USA TODAY. None of the individuals were vaccinated, USA TODAY reports. The first two measles deaths were the first in Pennsylvania in 35 years, the state Department of Health said in an Aug. 25 news release, and the first such deaths in the United States this year, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. Measles cases on the rise as Ohio vaccination rates fluctuate in state, U.S. Vaccination rates for measles have declined in recent years, resulting in a growing number of states no longer reporting rates consistent with herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when more than 95% of people in a community are vaccinated. Most people are then protected, even if they cannot get the vaccine themselves, because those around them are immune and cannot spread the disease. Vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners decreased from 95.2% during the 2019–20 school year to 92.5% in the 2024–25 school year, well under the threshold necessary for effective herd immunity, according to the CDC. Ohio's vaccination rate for the 2025-26 school year slipped well below the herd immunity threshold, making it susceptible to outbreaks. In Ohio, MMR vaccine — which protects against measles, mumps and rubella — coverage rate for children and adolescents was 91.5% for 2023. Previous years ranged from an 80% to 90% immunization rate: 2019: 81.8% 2020: 88.0% 2021: 91.7% 2022: 89.0% Declining protections have also been attributed to the growing anti-vaccine movement, which was bolstered by the confirmation of vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary. In addition to making anti-vaccine comments, Kennedy also downplayed pediatric deaths related to measles and touted false cures and preventive measures, such as the use of vitamin A. During the height of the Texas outbreak, Kennedy encouraged inoculation against measles, pulling back from his previous anti-vaccine messaging. Kennedy is now encouraging the measles vaccine. Trump signs executive order to separate MMR vaccine President Donald Trump in August 2026 signed an executive order to split the childhood measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into three shots and delivering them at separate medical visits as well as "calling for more vaccine flexibility and research" and fewer childhood vaccinations, according to USA TODAY. "You have the MMR, we want it in three separate vaccinations, given at separate times. Together there could be a possibility they're quite lethal and separately, it looks like they are not at all lethal, but just very effective," said Trump from the Oval Office as he signed the order. But the MMR vaccine is not lethal, and medical research shows no health benefit or reduced risk from splitting it. In contrast, separating the shots increases injection pain, leaves children unprotected longer, and lowers overall vaccination rates, according to experts. The MMR vaccine has been in existence since 1971, according to the World Health Organization. Measles cases hit 35-year high in United States The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000 after recording just 86 cases that year, according to USA TODAY, citing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. But a series of outbreaks that began in early 2025, centered initially in Gaines County, Texas, has helped drive the virus' resurgence. Health experts say the recent surge has been fueled by declining vaccination rates that have left more communities vulnerable to outbreaks. Can you get measles if vaccinated? Two doses of MMR are 97% effective against measles, ODH reports. If you are up to date on the measles vaccine, the risk of getting sick is very low. Are measles deadly? Measles can be deadly. ODH states that complications from measles are more common among children younger than 5 years of age, adults older than 20 years of age, pregnant women, and people with compromised immune systems. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. What does measles look like? Signs, symptoms Symptoms usually appear seven to 14 days after exposure, but it can take up to 21 days. Symptoms include a rash, high fever, runny nose, cough, loss of appetite and red, watery eyes. The rash usually lasts five to six days and begins at the hairline, moves to the face and upper neck, and proceeds down the body. Diarrhea and ear infections are common complications of measles. More severe complications such as pneumonia and encephalitis, a swelling of the brain, may also occur. The measles virus can live for up to two hours in air where an infected person coughed or sneezed. If other people breathe the contaminated air or touch an infected surface and then touch their eyes, noses, or mouths, they can become infected. People infected with measles can spread it to others from four days before through four days after a rash appears. Are measles itchy? Not usually, according to the Cleveland Clinic. How to protect yourself against measles Both ODH and the CDC say the best way to protect yourself against measles is to be vaccinated. USA TODAY reporters James Powel and Mary Walrath-Holdridge contributed to this report. supplementary_news.content: News Sports Business Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Grant County infant's death from measles is first in Wisconsin since 1990 Madeline Heim Milwaukee Journal Sentinel Nov. 5, 2026Updated Nov. 6, 2026, 6:07 a.m. CT A Grant County infant died of measles as southwest Wisconsin's outbreak continues to spread, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services and the Grant County Health Department have reported. The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles, according to a Nov. 5 news release pushed out midday by the department. It is the first measles death in the state since 1990. Grant County health officer Kessa Klaas said in her department's news release that the infant was too young to be vaccinated. "We need to take this time to work to protect one another," Klaas said. Wisconsin now joins Pennsylvania and New York in reporting measles deaths this year, once unthinkable because the U.S. had reduced transmission of the disease to negligible levels by 2000. But as vaccination rates for measles have slipped, outbreaks have erupted across the country, especially in the last two years. Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 2026, the most the state has seen in more than 35 years. Nine people have been hospitalized. All but three cases have been in people who did not received the measles vaccine, which is 97% effective at preventing infection. Disease transmission has primarily occurred in Amish and Mennonite communities. Cases were first reported to the public in early August, but data from the state health department show people first began experiencing symptoms in early July. A doctor and nurse who treat the Amish population in southwest Wisconsin confirmed to the Journal Sentinel that the disease came to the state after a large group traveled to Pennsylvania earlier this summer. Nearly one in five Wisconsin counties has seen a measles case this year, with the largest case counts still being reported in Grant, Lafayette and Iowa counties in the southwest part of the state. Nationally, multiple measles deaths this year have been in infants, who are particularly susceptible to complications from the disease. On Nov. 3, the state health department recommended that babies 6 months and older who are likely to be exposed to measles receive what's known as a "zero dose" of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine to offer protection before they can receive their first regular dose between 12 and 15 months of age. Between 500 and 600 of those zero doses have been given to Wisconsin infants since August, Stephanie Schauer, immunization program manager for the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, said in a Nov. 5 media briefing. They are not all related to the outbreak, Schauer said, because some are given to babies who are traveling internationally. Overall, officials said the state health department has delivered more than 2,000 doses of the measles vaccine to local health departments responding to the outbreak, and that more than 42,000 doses of the vaccine have been administered across the state since August. To get the state's outbreak under control, families need to make sure that both children and adults are up to date on their measles vaccine, and people need to recognize the symptoms of measles early, said chief medical officer and state epidemiologist Dr. Ryan Westergaard. "If we do things right, we can have a world where no one dies of measles," Westergaard said. "That's what we're aiming at." What are the symptoms of measles? Measles symptoms typically start a week to two weeks after infection with a high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes. A few days after the first symptoms arise, red spots or bumps appear on the face and near the hairline. That rash will spread to the rest of the body. People may also get tiny white spots inside the mouth a few days after symptoms begin. If you think you may have measles, avoid others and call a doctor's office or clinic before showing up to receive medical attention. Where to get a measles vaccine Wisconsin residents can check their measles, mumps and rubella vaccination status by visiting the Wisconsin Immunization Registry at dhfswir.org. The measles vaccine is covered by most insurance plans and is available at doctors' offices, local health departments, pharmacies and pop-up vaccine clinics. Those who need assistance affording vaccines can access them through the Vaccines for Children and Vaccines for Adults programs. This story has been updated to include new information. Madeline Heim covers health and the environment for the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. Contact her at 920-996-7266 or mheim@usatodayco.com. Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/AP View image in fullscreen Doctors work at the non-profit Union Community Care clinic, in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/AP ‘It’s clear they are under-vaccinated’: Amish under spotlight amid Pennsylvania measles outbreak As Josh Shapiro, the governor, mounts outreach program, members say ‘you don’t get to change anybody’s mind’ Making hay was more than a figure of speech last week at the New Holland auction house in Pennsylvania last week, where a ton of top quality hay bales were going for upwards of $400, up about 20% from last year. For members of the Lancaster settlement, a term used to describe the Amish population that came here in 1760, the price of hay was only part of the discussion: the price of horses, donkeys and milk were also topics of conversation and, as it has been for year or more, a potentially deadly outbreak of measles. At the most recent count, 1,398 cases had been detected, according to the Pennsylvania department of health. Since 1 August, 150,000 doses of the MMR vaccine had been administered, with more than 50,000 given in October alone. Families in the US are opting for earlier measles vaccinations amid outbreak Read more The outbreak, and the politics surrounding it under Robert F Kennedy Jr, the health secretary, has focused on Lancaster county, placing the Amish under a spotlight. While there is no Amish religious opposition to vaccines broadly, a study found that that less that a third of Amish residents had been immunized against measles, mumps and rubella. “It wasn’t that way 50 years ago in our community,” said Christ Stoltzfoos, standing outside a barn of horses, miniature ponies and donkeys that were also up for auction. But Stoltzfoos did not have a ready explanation for why vaccinations had lapsed in the community, which is descended from German-speaking religious conservatives and where the modern world is largely kept at bay. All of his immediate family had been vaccinated, and had not got sick, but some cousins had not been vaccinated and did, Stoltzfoos said. “I guess you don’t get to change anybody’s mind. The people that changed their mind are the people who got really sick from it. They say now they would have gotten vaccinated. But the people that didn’t really get sick, they still say: ‘Oh, it’s not really that bad.’” View image in fullscreen A hay auction at The Green Dragon Farmers Market and Auction in Ephrata, Pennsylvania, on 9 October 2026. Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/AP The attention the Amish have received while experiencing the worst outbreak in the nation has not always been welcome. But the state, under Josh Shapiro, the Democratic governor, has mounted an intensive outreach of pop-up clinics and mailings to encourage the community to get protection. The Lancaster settlement depends in large part on tourism, with coachloads of visitors stopping to buy shoofly pie and other Amish delicacies. Vaccination is thus, in part, a business decision. Still, almost two-thirds of measles cases in Pennsylvania have been among adults, a mirror opposite of how measles is typically transmitted. All five of the Pennsylvania mortalities involved people who were unvaccinated by choice or because they were too young to receive it, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer. But within the Lancaster community, vaccines don’t necessarily carry the politicization of the “English” world. “A lot of people now get the shots,” Stoltzfoos said. Nearby, John Kaufman, 81, was operating from a different playbook. He said the vaccine was hard on the immune system. “You get the measles and you get over it. People have it once, and it’s over. But if you hurt your immune system with the shots, something else will creep up on. The shot will take care of the measles, but it’ll stir something else up. Then what?” He pointed to reports that Covid shots had been linked to heart attacks and, he said, cancer: “If you’re strong and healthy you might be able to work the Covid shot off. But if you had a weakness in yourself, it could take over.” View image in fullscreen Measles, mumps and rubella virus vaccine at Union Community Care clinic in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/AP Anna, a young woman at the auction, also said she had had measles. “It was miserable,” she said. “My whole family had it, except my dad. He got the vaccine. I wouldn’t get the vaccine now because if you had measles, you’re stronger for it. Why change that?” The thinking around the measles vaccine in the community is in some ways a reflection of thinking in the “English” world beyond, where health authorities are battling outbreaks in South Carolina and Texas for much of the last year. But those outbreaks primarily affect children. Pennsylvania has recorded five measles-associated deaths (including two infants and three adults with underlying health conditions), but those numbers are not reflected in CDC data, which records three deaths nationwide of 4,588 confirmed cases in 2026. This month Kennedy, who heads the vaccine-skeptic Maha movement, claimed that the “people of Pennsylvania suffered” because Shapiro’s administration politicized the state’s measles outbreak. Kennedy said that a “global measles outbreak” had been caused by decline in the number of people receiving the measles vaccine during Covid. Pennsylvania, which has 27% of US cases, had only begun applying for CDC emergency assistance in September. But Shapiro claimed that the CDC would not correctly acknowledge the measles-related deaths “because it doesn’t fit their phony narrative. I think RFK is doing great destruction in this country by stoking this vaccine skepticism.” The state has sent 300 health department staff to the area and administered nearly 6,000 vaccinations. View image in fullscreen Children from the Plain community play on a trampoline in Intercourse, Pennsylvania. Photograph: Jessie Wardarski/AP Vaccination politics has also reached the race for Pennsylvania’s 11th congressional district, where five-term Republican representative Lloyd Smucker is being challenged by Democrat Nancy Mannion. At a town hall-style debate last week, Smucker, who was raised Amish until he was five, said the Amish are making decisions they think are best for their families. “The role of government should be to do research and development on vaccines and be open and transparent about what that means. It was disappointing to me to see the governor using the measles to score political points,” he said. “It turns out that the first two deaths really weren’t caused by measles at all.” But Mannion, a former emergency nurse and international healthcare leader, told the Guardian: “The Amish aren’t anti-vaccination, but they don’t access the healthcare system in the same way. It’s not just the Amish that are part of this outbreak because of the skepticism has brought to vaccines I would tie directly back to Robert Kennedy Jr.” Measles, Mannion said, “is completely preventable and had been eradicated, but now we’re living in a surge. I’d say there is a link between his anti-vaccine stance generally and what were seeing now.” The Amish in Lancaster are not the only such community to experience larger political forces. In upstate New York, the state health department has been battling three small Amish schools over whether the children fall under immunization rules or should be granted an exemption on freedom of religious practice grounds. Kathy Hochul, the New York governor, recently declared a statewide health emergency after more than 100 people contracted measles, an outbreak epidemiologists believe is connected to the outbreak in Pennsylvania and also one in Ohio. The schools now face fines of $2,000 per unvaccinated student. Steven Nolt, professor of history and Anabaptist studies at Elizabethtown College, points out that it is by family tradition and not religious instruction that the Amish accept or decline immunizations. At the same time, he said, there is some evidence that vaccine-skeptical groups had been doing outreach to the Amish since 2015. But accurate information is hard to come by, he says. “We don’t have good data but it’s clear they are under-vaccinated, but by how much we don’t know. The Amish are a religious group, so governments are not allowed to track information. We don’t know any better how many Amish are immunized than how many Anglicans or Presbyterians are immunized.” At the New Holland auction, the measles question was in fact less pressing than land values, interest rates, and the costs of diesel, hay and livestock. The Amish are to some extent protected from the price of fuel because they use horses in the fields, but also exposed because of their use of diesel-powered generators, pickers and milking machines. A shift in farming practices, from crops and livestock to milk and vegetables, also presented changes, and many had moved away from agriculture to furniture-making and construction. Dairy prices were way down but organic milk was a good business, Christ and his uncle Amos Stoltzfoos agreed, with 100lbs fetching $51. “We’re at their mercy but I don’t feel that we’re wrongly used,” Christ said of the milk companies. But sales of raw milk, illegal to consumers in New York have also become an outside political issue. “I think it’s good they regulate raw milk or it will be like the measles soon,” Christ Stoltzfoos said. Both agreed that the Amish don’t like to deal directly with the government. “Most of us don’t even know what’s going on,” the younger man said. “I read the paper but that don’t tell me much.” Explore more on these topics Pennsylvania MMR Health US healthcare US politics features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Live Democrats blast Trump’s decision to appoint Stephen Miller as chief of staff in wake of Republican midterm rout – live Incoming Democratic senators don’t want Chuck Schumer as majority leader Lawyers descend on Mississippi as vote counting continues in razor-thin Senate race Famous New Mexico rock formation destroyed after torrential El Niño rains Martin Rowson on the aftermath of the US midterm elections – cartoon Most viewed Most viewed

ByABC7 Chicago Digital Team Thursday, November 5, 2026 6:52PM Share CHICAGO (WLS) -- An infant has died from the measles in Wisconsin, local health officials said Thursday. It's the first death of its kind reported in the state since 1990. ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch Health officials said the death is connected to an ongoing measles outbreak in southwestern Wisconsin. As of Tuesday, health officials reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far in 2026. It's the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years. Wisconsin Reports Its First Infant Death Linked To Measles In 36 Years The death immediately follows Pennsylvania reporting its sixth measles-associated death this year, and New York reporting its first. Siddhi Mahatole Nov 6, 2026, 08:49 AM EST Leave a Comment LOADINGERROR LOADING The Wisconsin Department of Health Services said on Thursday that an infant had died in connection with the ongoing measles outbreak in the state. The coroner listed measles as the immediate cause of death, the department said, declining to release further details to protect the family’s privacy. Advertisement The death comes as the United States faces its highest number of measles cases in decades, fueled by outbreaks in several states and declining childhood vaccination rates in some communities. Wisconsin had reported 431 cases across 13 counties as of November 3, with nine people hospitalized for severe symptoms. Advertisement “This is the largest number of measles cases we’ve seen in Wisconsin in more than 35 years,” state epidemiologist Ryan Westergaard said in a media call. “The 431 cases we’ve identified are almost certainly an underestimate. Not everyone who becomes infected gets tested or comes to the attention of public health,” he added. A fact sheet for measles sits on a table at a mobile clinic offering free vaccinations in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Sean Rayford via Getty Images Advertisement State health officials said they have worked with local and Tribal health departments to respond to the outbreak through case tracking, testing and vaccination efforts. The Department of Health and Human Services did not immediately respond to Reuters for comment. On Wednesday, Pennsylvania health officials reported the state’s sixth measles-associated death this year. While New York state reported its first measles-associated child death earlier this week. Pediatric healthcare workers assess a patient with measles symptoms in Spartanburg, South Carolina, in January. The Washington Post via Getty Images Advertisement However, the CDC has recorded four measles-related deaths this year but did not name the states where they occurred. The gap in numbers follows a policy shift under US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., with the CDC switching to the National Center for Health Statistics’ mortality data to track measles deaths, replacing its earlier reliance on state health departments’ figures. Wisconsin infant is US’ third measles-related death this week Children's health Vaccines See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! US states have announced eight deaths related to measles so far in 2026. Callista Images/Image Source/Getty Images An infant in Wisconsin has died in connection with an large, ongoing measles outbreak, the state health department said Thursday. The death marks the first measles-related death in Wisconsin in more than 35 years and the third reported in the US this week. “My heart is broken for the family,” said Kirsten Johnson, secretary of the state’s health department. “Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family.” The health department said the coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles. To protect the family’s privacy, the department will not release any additional details about the child, officials said. Ad Feedback Wisconsin is experiencing its largest measles outbreak in more than three decades. As of Thursday, Wisconsin has recorded 431 cases in 13 counties this years. The state’s health department cautions that the true number is most certainly higher because not everyone who gets sick seeks medical care. To compare, Wisconsin had 36 cases in 2025. In the past, most cases were associated with international travel. Now, cases are now spreading through domestic travel, as well as through exposure to family members and others in the community. Nine people in Wisconsin have been hospitalized. While anyone with measles can develop life-threatening complications such as pneumonia or swelling of the brain, children younger than 5, people with weak immune systems and people who are pregnant face a higher risk of severe disease. The state is encouraging everyone who hasn’t been vaccinated to receive a measles vaccine. Two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are 97% effective at preventing measles. Health officials said the rate of MMR vaccination among kindergarteners in Wisconsin is at about 85%, well below the roughly 95% coverage needed to prevent measles from spreading through a population. “That’s really the central issue here: Measles is now spreading because there are enough people who are susceptible to infection for the virus to continue finding new hosts,” said Dr. Ryan Westergaard, Wisconsin’s chief medical officer and state epidemiologist for communicable diseases. Wisconsin’s health department updated its guidance this week to recommend an early dose of MMR vaccine for certain infants between 6 and 11 months of age who are at increased risk of exposure during the outbreak. Typically, MMR vaccination doesn’t start until a child’s first birthday. Related article A measles alert sign hangs outside the entrance to the Cohen Children's Medical Center in New Hyde Park, New York, U.S., March 14, 2025. Shannon Stapleton/Reuters/File Child in New York dies after contracting measles, the state’s first such death in 30 years 4 min read Until 2025, there had been no measles deaths in the US for years. Three measles-related deaths have already been reported this week. In Pennsylvania, an unvaccinated resident of rural Jefferson County, in the north-central part of the state, died after testing positive for measles, the Pennsylvania Department of Health said on Wednesday. It was the sixth person in Pennsylvania to die from measles this year. On Monday, the New York State Department of Health announced that a child had died after contracting measles. The child lived in rural Lewis County, in the northern part of the state. The child’s death marked New York’s first in 30 years. More than 4,800 measles cases have been reported across the US this year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — the most since 1991, almost a decade before measles was declared eliminated in the US. An international meeting to determine the status of measles elimination in the United States is scheduled to take place next week.
